name: Lookback
one_liner: Upload the 60 months of bank, brokerage and financial statements behind a long-term-care Medicaid application and get back the three artifacts the caseworker actually adjudicates: a month-by-account statement-completeness matrix, a line-cited uncompensated-transfer schedule, and a state-specific penalty-exposure estimate — every flagged line linked to a crop of the source page.
product_form: Standalone web app (no extension). Drag a folder of PDFs/scans onto the page, pick the state and application date; 20-40 minutes later you get an XLSX + PDF exhibit set and an interactive review grid where each flagged transaction sits next to an image crop of the statement line it came from, with accept/recategorize buttons. Card on file, per-file pricing, no demo, no sales call.
ai_core: Three-stage pipeline. (1) Vision-language extraction: each scanned/faxed statement page is parsed to structured transactions + account header + statement period. Frontier-class VLM for this — Claude Haiku 4.5 (batch $0.50/MTok in, $2.50/MTok out, fetched 2026-08-20) handles the bulk; ambiguous or badly-scanned pages escalate to Sonnet 5 (batch $1/$5). (2) A fine-tuned specialized classifier does the vertical work: every transaction line is labeled into Medicaid-eligibility classes — uncompensated transfer candidate / transfer to exempt recipient (spouse, disabled child, caregiver-child, sibling with equity) / medical or LTC expense / ordinary living expense / income deposit / internal transfer between the applicant's own accounts / unexplained cash withdrawal above the state's scrutiny threshold. Base model: an open 7-8B vision-capable model (Qwen-VL / Llama-class) fine-tuned, so the per-line pass is near-zero marginal cost. Dataset to assemble, autonomously: (a) ~200 top US bank/brokerage statement layouts reproduced as synthetic generators with scan/fax degradation, yielding ~500k labeled transaction lines whose ground truth is known by construction because we generated it; (b) programmatic labeling of the Medicaid classes from the transaction's own structured fields (payee string, amount, recurrence, counterparty match against the applicant's other accounts) using rules distilled from state eligibility manuals, then verified against a held-out human-labeled set; (c) the compounding set — every attorney recategorization in the product is a label, written back with the page crop. (3) Deterministic layer, not the model: the month x account completeness grid, penalty math (transfer total / state divisor), and the RFV deadline calendar are code, so the highest-consequence outputs carry no model uncertainty at all.
why_now: Two capabilities, both post-2023. First, vision-language parsing of heterogeneous scanned/faxed financial statements: a 60-month Medicaid file is 400-700 pages of statements from a dozen institutions, half of them faxed or photographed, in layouts no fixed template covers — pre-2023 OCR + regex pipelines could not read them, which is exactly why the work is still done by a paralegal with a highlighter. Second, price. Claude Haiku 4.5 batch input is $0.50/MTok as of the pricing page fetched 2026-08-20; a 600-page file is roughly 1.1M vision-input tokens, so the whole read costs single-digit dollars. At 2022 prices the same read would have cost more than the paralegal.
buyer: Primary: elder law firms and Medicaid-planning practices that file long-term-care Medicaid applications on flat fees. NAELA membership is ~4,400-5,000 attorneys (searched 2026-08-20), and the addressable set is larger — non-attorney Medicaid planners and application-preparation companies (e.g. Medicaid Plus, serving PA/NJ/DE/MD, fetched 2026-08-20) do the same work. Secondary and larger: skilled-nursing and assisted-living business offices, who carry the A/R risk on 'Medicaid pending' residents — 1.3M people used Medicaid nursing facility care in 2021 and ~56% of nursing home residents are Medicaid-covered (KFF, searched 2026-08-20), and every one of them was applied for. Self-serve reachable: these are 2-20 person practices that already buy $269/mo software with a credit card (Relaw's own published price, fetched 2026-08-20).
market_evidence: Money is already changing hands for this exact labor, at high prices, done by humans. (1) Elder law firms charge $6,000-$15,000 flat for Medicaid planning and application, with one firm quoting $6,500-$8,500 'to apply for Medicaid benefits from start to finish' (searched 2026-08-20) — and the dominant labor line inside that fee is a paralegal reading five years of statements. (2) The closest software proxy for the labor's value: CounselPro sells AI bank-statement forensics to legal teams at '$499 a matter' (fetched 2026-08-20). Firms are demonstrably willing to pay ~$500 per matter to have statements read by a machine — CounselPro just doesn't sell into Medicaid. (3) The denial risk that makes it urgent: Florida requires a 'complete five-year asset transfer disclosure' with the ICP application, and DCF's Request for Verification gives 10-30 days to close gaps or the application is denied and restarted while the nursing home bill accrues (searched 2026-08-20). (4) Caseworker behavior is documented: agencies flag unexplained withdrawals, compare deposits against known income, and 'usually request explanations for all expenditures that exceed $500' inside the look-back (searched 2026-08-20) — i.e. the deliverable we generate is precisely the artifact the adjudicator demands.
incumbents: Five closest, all with fetched prices, none doing this job. (1) Relaw.ai — the self-described premier AI elder-law platform, $269/mo Standard / $349/mo Pro (fetched 2026-08-20). Decisive: its own competitive guide states no tool in the category analyzes bank statements for the 5-year look-back, and Relaw explicitly disclaims 'automated Medicaid eligibility engines,' saying its role is 'collecting facts, organizing documents, drafting from your templates.' The category leader publicly declines this job. (2) CounselPro — $499/matter, AI forensic bank-statement analysis, 10,000+ institutions, source-linked reports (fetched 2026-08-20). Practice areas listed: bankruptcy, family law, accounting, estate planning, probate, business litigation. No mention of Medicaid, elder law, or eligibility rules. It indexes and traces money; it does not know what a penalty divisor is. This is the real threat and the real gap. (3) Estateably — fiduciary/estate accounting, pay-per-file $179 estate accounting / $198 trust accounting, and it does use AI to scan financial statements to build asset schedules (searched 2026-08-20; homepage fetched 2026-08-20 shows no Medicaid or look-back content). Closest adjacent technology, different statutory output. (4) DocuClipper — $20 / $111 / $360 per month for 60 / 640 / 2,000 pages, statements to CSV/QBO (fetched 2026-08-20). Pure extraction, zero rules; it would hand the paralegal a spreadsheet and leave 100% of the classification work. (5) Ocrolus — publishes on standardizing Medicaid document processing, but sells to the payer/agency side of eligibility, not the applicant's counsel (searched 2026-08-20). Also checked and cleared: InPractice ($0.05/page) and Superinsight (SSD page, no price shown) are medical-records-only and state no financial-document capability (both fetched 2026-08-20); four separate targeted searches for a look-back bank-statement tool returned no product.
moat: Not the prompt. Three compounding assets. (1) The 51-jurisdiction rule corpus: look-back length (60 months standard; California reinstating 60 months for nursing homes in 2026; New York community Medicaid still 0 with a 30-month plan pending), penalty divisor with effective date (Florida $10,645/mo eff. 4/1/2025; Pennsylvania $12,811.50/mo = $421.20/day for 2026; Texas $242.13/day eff. 9/1/25; Massachusetts $450/day eff. 11/1/25-10/31/26; New York regional $13,765-$15,675), asset limits, exempt-transfer categories, state scrutiny thresholds (PA tolerates $500/month gifting), and each state's verification checklist and RFV deadline. Divisors change on staggered per-state schedules — Arkansas and New Jersey in April, Connecticut and Indiana in July, Massachusetts in November (all fetched 2026-08-20). A generalist model is wrong about these constantly and cannot tell you it is wrong. (2) The fine-tuned line classifier plus its eval harness: a held-out set of statement pages with known-correct transfer schedules, scored on recall of uncompensated transfers (the expensive miss) and precision on exempt-transfer classification, published per state. That harness is the thing a chat interface can never produce, and it is what lets us make a refund promise. (3) Usage-accumulated labels: every recategorization an attorney makes is a supervised example tied to a page crop, and elder law firms see the same regional banks and the same payee strings repeatedly, so per-state accuracy compounds with volume.
inference_economics: A 600-page file at ~1,800 vision tokens/page is ~1.08M input tokens. Haiku 4.5 batch: 1.08M x $0.50/MTok = $0.54 input; structured transaction output at ~600 tokens/page = 360k x $2.50/MTok = $0.90. Escalating ~15% of pages to Sonnet 5 batch ($1/$5) adds ~$0.75. The per-line Medicaid classification runs on the fine-tuned 7-8B model on our own GPU — effectively zero marginal cost, and the reason for fine-tuning rather than calling a frontier model 5,000 times. All-in $2-5 per file against a $199 price: 97%+ gross margin, and the margin holds even if we never ship the fine-tune and run everything on Sonnet 5 (~$10-12/file). Local WebGPU is deliberately not the answer here — 600 scanned pages exceeds what a browser-resident small model can read accurately, and the privacy wedge is served instead by a no-retention processing mode and per-file deletion.
autonomy_case: A1: card-swipe signup, drag-and-drop, no demo path exists in the product. A2: fulfilment is the pipeline; nobody touches a file. A3 is the design centre, because this output sits next to a benefits denial. The product never asserts 'this is a penalized transfer.' It emits candidates with (i) an image crop of the source line and its page number, (ii) a model confidence, (iii) the state rule and effective date it was measured against, and (iv) a required-attorney-review flag on anything below threshold, which lands in a separate 'unresolved' schedule rather than the main exhibit. The two highest-consequence numbers — the completeness grid and the penalty arithmetic — are deterministic code over extracted metadata, not model judgment. When statement coverage is too poor to support a schedule at all, the run aborts before billing and refunds automatically rather than shipping a confident-looking wrong exhibit. A4: the rule corpus is rebuilt on a schedule by re-crawling state eligibility manuals and divisor publications, with a diff alert and an effective-date stamp shown on every output; a stale state is shown as stale rather than silently used. A5: batch API, queue, retries. A6: zero human minutes — the recategorization UI means the customer, not us, resolves the ambiguous tail, and their resolution is our training label.
pricing_hypothesis: $199 per case file up to 750 pages ($0.20/page beyond), which deliberately undercuts CounselPro's $499/matter for generic statement forensics while doing the vertical work it doesn't. Practice plan at $399/mo for 4 files plus $99 each thereafter, aimed at firms filing 3-8 applications a month. Free forever: the statement-completeness matrix for a single account (the deterministic half) — it costs us cents, it is the fastest demonstration that we can read their client's terrible fax, and it is the wedge that gets the folder uploaded.
distribution: Zero-human channels only. (1) SEO against a corpus we must maintain anyway: an always-current, per-state look-back and penalty-divisor reference with effective dates and change history — the exact pages people search ('Florida Medicaid penalty divisor 2026', 'PA 5 year look back bank statements'). The reference data is the moat and the traffic at once, and it self-updates, so the SEO surface grows without us. (2) Free-tier wedge: the one-account completeness checker and a 'what will DCF ask me to explain' scan. (3) Communities where these buyers already are: NAELA sections and state chapters, ElderLawAnswers, Medicaid-planner Facebook groups, and AAPACN/business-office forums on the SNF side. AP1 answered: this is not a question a $20 chat subscription answers — it is 600 scanned pages producing a deterministic month x account grid, a per-line schedule with image citations, and arithmetic against 51 divisors with staggered effective dates that a generalist is silently stale on. AP2 answered: nothing here is 'summarize this page.' The unit of work is a folder, the deliverable is an XLSX exhibit filed with a state agency, and the browser's Gemini has no access to the folder, no eval on the classification, and no rule corpus.
risks: AP6: (a) Model deprecation and price moves — mitigated by a model-agnostic extraction layer and by the fact that the classification tier is our own weights; the retired-model list on Anthropic's own pricing page (fetched 2026-08-20) is a standing reminder to pin nothing. (b) Data handling is the real platform risk: these are a dying person's complete financial records. We need a click-through DPA, no-retention mode, and per-file deletion from day one; some records will contain incidental PHI. (c) State manual URL churn breaking the A4 crawler — mitigated by showing staleness rather than failing silently. Competitive: CounselPro is one product decision away — it already reads statements at $499/matter and already sells to estate planning and probate; our defence is the rule corpus, the per-state eval harness and the label flywheel, none of which it can buy. NOT YET PROVEN, honestly: (1) whether small elder law firms will upload client financial records to a third-party SaaS without a negotiated vendor agreement — this is the single biggest unknown and it is a sales-friction question that could break A1; (2) whether the synthetic-statement dataset generalizes to real faxed statements well enough that the fine-tune beats a frontier generalist — until the eval harness says yes, we ship on frontier models and the moat is only the rule corpus; (3) whether firms that have already sunk the paralegal salary will pay per file rather than absorb the hours; (4) that the SNF business-office segment pays at all — I found no fetched evidence of facilities buying per-application services, so that segment is a hypothesis, not a finding.

name: Markline
one_liner: A browser-resident, fully offline scanner that reads a defense contractor's own file shares, finds the documents that carry or derive from Controlled Unclassified Information, applies the DoD-prescribed banner/footer/designation markings, and emits a CUI inventory and marking-decision register — with nothing ever leaving the machine, because sending that data to a cloud AI is a DFARS violation.
product_form: Browser-resident app (local WebGPU/WASM inference, no server round-trip), delivered as a signed offline HTML+model bundle that also runs from a USB stick on an air-gapped workstation. UX: the user picks a folder (File System Access API, or `<input webkitdirectory>` fallback), watches a live progress table as thousands of files are parsed, OCR'd and scored locally, then works a triage queue of three buckets — Marked correctly / Mismarked / Unmarked-candidate — each row quoting the exact trigger text and the CUI Registry category it maps to. One click writes correctly-marked copies (banner, footer, designation indicator block, portion marks where required) and exports the CUI inventory spreadsheet plus a per-file evidence log.
ai_core: Three small specialized models, all local. (1) Document understanding: a SmolDocling-256M-class image-text-to-text model (256M LM + ~93M vision encoder) via transformers.js with `device: 'webgpu'`, converting scanned drawings, TDPs, scanned contract PDFs and screenshots into structured text with bounding boxes — needed because drawings and legacy scans are exactly where markings hide. (2) CUI-indicator detection: a fine-tuned encoder token-classifier (~150-400M params, ONNX int8) that detects distribution statements, export-control notices, DFARS/FAR clause references, designation indicator blocks, CDRL/DD-254 references, and technical-data attributes, and maps each to a NARA CUI Registry category. (3) mxbai-embed-xsmall-class embeddings for near-duplicate clustering so a 40,000-file share collapses to a few thousand distinct decisions. Model strategy is deliberately FINE-TUNED, not frontier API: the frontier API is contractually unavailable for this data (see AP1), so the model must be small enough to run on the customer's own GPU. Dataset assembled autonomously: DTIC's public technical-report corpus (every report carries a Distribution Statement A-F on its face), SAM.gov solicitation attachments, GSA/DoD CUI program guides, and the NARA CUI Registry category definitions — all crawlable by code, and self-labeling, because the marking printed on the document IS the label. Target ~300k-1M pages of (page image, text, marking) triples, zero human annotation, refreshed on a schedule.
why_now: Three capabilities, none of which existed before ~2023. (a) WebGPU is now mainstream — caniuse shows 85.56% global support as of the July 2026 usage data, Chrome/Edge 113+, Safari 26+, and transformers.js exposes it with a one-line `device: 'webgpu'` switch (HF docs, fetched 2026-08-20). (b) Sub-400M document-understanding VLMs that actually OCR and lay out documents now exist and have shipped as working in-browser builds — SmolDocling-256M-preview with a public WebGPU implementation running entirely on-device. (c) The pain became acute in 2026: Federal News Network, August 2026, reports that industry groups named inconsistent CUI identification and marking a primary cost driver of the CMMC program, and that the SBA Office of Advocacy called CUI uncertainty 'the most frequently cited concern' for small businesses — with the quoted contractor behaviour being 'when a contractor cannot confidently determine what information is CUI, they will generally err on the side of including all of it.' Over-scoping is the expensive mistake this product exists to reverse.
buyer: US defense-industrial-base contractors and subcontractors, weighted to the 10-250-employee machine shops, engineering firms and integrators who receive CUI via contract flow-down and have no security staff. DoD's own 32 CFR CMMC rule estimated the CUI-level requirements would apply to roughly 65% of the DIB (search-surfaced 2026-08-20). Self-serve reachability is already proven in this exact segment: Totem Technologies sells CMMC compliance software to micro-contractors at roughly $265/month on a published price page — a card-swipe purchase, no procurement. Secondary buyer: the MSPs and Registered Practitioner shops that serve dozens of these contractors and would run the scan as a repeatable engagement.
market_evidence: Money is already changing hands for worse solutions to the same job. (1) Totem Tech: ~$265/mo self-serve CMMC tooling for small DIB firms (totem.tech pricing page, surfaced 2026-08-20) — proves the segment buys software with a card at ~$3.2k/yr. (2) The cost of getting scoping wrong is directly priced: Microsoft 365 G3 GCC High reseller planning price is $65.20/user/month as of the 1 July 2026 government pricing update (Secureframe GCC High pricing guide, 2026-08-20). A firm that over-scopes and puts 40 people in GCC High instead of 12 burns ~$21,900/year in avoidable licences — Markline's entire value proposition is a defensible, evidenced narrowing of that footprint. (3) The downside is priced too: on 18 June 2026 DOJ settled with defense contractor LOGZONE Inc. for $507,144 under the Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative over failure to satisfy contractual cybersecurity requirements, and notably it came from a government-initiated DIBCAC assessment rather than a whistleblower (Sidley FCA Blog, 2026-06-23). FCA settlements exceeded $6.8B in FY2025. (4) Enterprise data-classification suites (Fortra/Titus) sell CUI-specific marking today, but only into organisations large enough to buy an enterprise classification platform.
incumbents: Five closest, each with the gap named. (1) **Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels + auto-labeling** — the most serious. Content marking (headers/footers/watermarks) and auto-labeling exist, but Microsoft Learn's own auto-labeling doc requires Microsoft 365 E5/A5/G5 or E5 Compliance, and non-M365 data sources require E5 plus pay-as-you-go billing; every user with access to a processed site needs a licence. In GCC High that is $65.20/user/mo before the compliance uplift. It also only sees data already inside M365 — not the engineering NAS, the CAM workstation, or the shop-floor PC where drawings actually live, and it is useless for the pre-migration question 'which of my files are CUI, so how big does my enclave need to be?'. (2) **Fortra Data Classification Suite (ex-Titus)** — explicitly markets preconfigured CUI classification with automatic marking on save/send, embedded as Office/Outlook add-ins; enterprise-quoted, no published price, historic Titus list was $29.99/user, and it is a user-prompted labeling product, not a retrospective discovery scan of existing archives. (3) **Kiteworks** — a Private Data Network for CUI governance and secure sharing; enterprise, sales-led, priced as a platform, and solves transport rather than 'what is CUI in the pile I already have.' (4) **IPKeys** — advertises automated CUI discovery and classification; enterprise/services engagement, no self-serve pricing published. (5) **Totem Technologies (~$265/mo)** — the incumbent the buyer already pays, but it is an SSP/POA&M/assessment-tracking tool; it does not scan files or apply markings, so it is a distribution partner more than a competitor. Notably absent from the entire field: any self-serve, per-company-priced tool that scans local file shares for CUI. Every search for one returns enterprise classification platforms and consultants. (Contrast the consumer-shaped local-AI niches — free browser-local tools have already colonised video face-blurring and bank-statement parsing; nobody has done this one, because the buyer is not reachable by an anonymous free web toy.)
moat: Not a prompt — the prompt is not even available (no cloud model may touch this data). The moat is (a) the assembled corpus: hundreds of thousands of real government/DIB pages whose own printed Distribution Statements, CUI banners and designation blocks provide free ground-truth labels, crawled and refreshed by code from DTIC and SAM.gov; (b) the fine-tuned detector trained on it, which recognises the visual and textual grammar of DoD markings (banner placement, portion-mark syntax, DD-254 references, distribution-statement boilerplate) that a generalist has never been optimised for; (c) a published eval harness — held-out documents with known markings, reported as precision/recall per CUI Registry category, versioned per model release. That harness is the thing a generalist chat can never produce: a contractor facing FCA exposure needs a number, not a vibe. (d) Usage-accumulated: every user correction in the triage queue is a labelled example the customer can optionally contribute back (default off, opt-in, and de-identified to marking-pattern level only — never document content).
inference_economics: Zero marginal inference cost by construction — all three models execute on the customer's GPU. Our only variable cost is one-time CDN egress of the model bundle (~400MB-900MB int8-quantised, cached in the browser after first load) at roughly $0.03-0.08 per install on commodity object storage, plus Stripe fees. At $149-399/month, gross margin is effectively 100% and does not degrade with usage — which is precisely the pricing weapon: we can offer unlimited files and unlimited re-scans where every cloud competitor must meter. For comparison, a cloud equivalent would pay per-page OCR plus per-character NER (AWS Comprehend Medical, fetched 2026-08-20, bills in units of 100 characters with a 1-unit minimum per request), so a 40,000-file archive re-scanned monthly is a real recurring cost line for them and a rounding error for us. Local also removes the FedRAMP-equivalency cost that any cloud competitor must carry.
autonomy_case: A1 self-serve: Stripe checkout, instant licence key, browser app — the DIB segment already buys this way (Totem, $265/mo, no calls). A2 fulfilment by code: the scan, the marking application and the report generation are the product; there is no service component. A3 no human escalation — and this is the design centre, because a wrong output here has False Claims Act consequence. Markline never asserts that a document is not CUI. It produces three buckets, and the 'unmarked-candidate' and 'uncertain' buckets are never silently cleared: each row quotes the exact trigger span, cites the NARA CUI Registry category and the DoDI 5200.48 marking rule that would apply, and shows a calibrated confidence. Below the confidence floor, the row is forced into 'review required' and is excluded from any count the report presents as settled. Every report carries a standing disclosure that CUI designation authority rests with the Government under 32 CFR 2002 and is conveyed by the contract/DD-254, that Markline propagates and checks markings rather than originating designations, and that the output is decision support and not a compliance certification. Degradation ladder: low confidence → narrow the claim to 'contains an indicator of category X'; no confident indicator → 'no indicator found — absence of an indicator is not evidence of non-CUI'; model can't parse the file (encrypted, exotic CAD) → listed as 'not analysed' in an explicit unprocessed-files appendix rather than counted as clean. Self-serve refund: the user can run a labelled sample of their own files; if measured precision falls below the published threshold, the app issues an automatic Stripe refund without contacting anyone. A4 self-maintaining reference data: the NARA CUI Registry, DoDI 5200.48 marking rules, and the DTIC/SAM.gov training corpus are all public and machine-fetchable on a schedule. A5/A6: no per-customer infrastructure exists at all — the customer's own machine is the compute — so unattended ops means keeping a static bundle online.
pricing_hypothesis: Free tier: single-document CUI marking checker, no signup, runs in the tab — the SEO and trust wedge. Shop tier $149/mo (or $1,490/yr) — up to 3 workstations, unlimited files, unlimited re-scans, marking application, inventory export. Program tier $399/mo — unlimited workstations, the scoping-evidence pack (inventory + boundary rationale + unprocessed-files appendix), and eval-harness report attached to each scan. One-off 'Scoping Scan' at $999 for firms that want the pre-enclave answer once. The pitch is arithmetic: $1,788/yr against ~$21,900/yr of avoidable GCC High seats at $65.20/user/mo.
distribution: Zero-human channels only. (1) SEO/answer-engine surface on the exact questions this buyer types — 'how to mark CUI', 'CUI banner marking example', 'is this CUI', 'CUI vs FOUO', 'CUI scoping' — each landing on a page whose call to action is the free in-browser checker, not a form. The August 2026 Federal News Network coverage confirms this is the most-searched confusion in the segment. (2) The free single-document checker itself: it runs with no signup and no upload, which is the only way this buyer will ever try an unknown tool with a marked document. (3) Communities that self-serve: r/CMMC, DIB LinkedIn groups, the Registered Practitioner/RPO ecosystem, CMMC-focused newsletters — all reachable by publishing the eval-harness numbers, which is content nobody else in this space publishes. (4) MSP/RPO reseller link with a self-serve multi-tenant key. AP1 addressed: ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini at $0-20/mo cannot do this for this user, and not for prompt reasons — DFARS 252.204-7012(b)(2)(ii)(D) requires any cloud service provider that stores, processes or transmits covered defense information to meet FedRAMP Moderate equivalency, and the December 2023 DoD memo closed the SOC-2-is-good-enough loophole. Pasting a CUI drawing into a consumer assistant is the prohibited act itself. Beyond that, the job is 40,000 files and a structured register, not one question. AP2 addressed: Chrome's built-in Gemini and agentic browsers are page-shaped — they summarise what is on screen and they do it by sending it to Google. The shape here is a batch sweep of a local NAS producing a marking register, and the whole point is that no browser AI touches the bytes.
risks: AP6 platform risk, stated plainly. (1) Regulatory whiplash: DoD suspended CMMC Phase 2 on 13 July 2026, freezing the C3PAO-certification-as-condition-of-award milestone. That deflates deadline-panic GTM. It is a policy pause, not a repeal — the CMMC Program rule stands, DFARS was not amended, NIST SP 800-171 has been a contract obligation since 2017, the DFARS 7019/7020 SPRS self-attestation still runs, and DOJ is still settling FCA cases off DIBCAC scores (LOGZONE, June 2026). The durable driver is the marking obligation plus FCA exposure, not the CMMC calendar — but urgency is measurably lower than it was in 2025 and the messaging must lead with cost (GCC High seats) rather than deadline. (2) DoD's own CUI guidance is inconsistent — which is the pain, but it also means ground truth drifts; the eval harness must be re-run against refreshed DTIC/registry data every release and the model version stamped on every report. (3) Browser platform: File System Access API / showDirectoryPicker is flagged 'limited availability, experimental' on MDN and is Chromium-only; the fallback is a directory upload input, which still keeps files local but degrades the folder-write step to a downloaded ZIP. Chrome could tighten local-filesystem permissions. (4) Microsoft is the real competitive risk: a G5-licensed contractor already has auto-labeling and content marking, and Microsoft could extend Purview discovery beyond M365. name: Safeharbor
one_liner: A zero-install, zero-upload browser workbench that de-identifies a folder of clinical notes, PDFs and spreadsheets on the researcher's own machine — removing the 18 HIPAA Safe Harbor identifiers with a clinical-domain model, keeping the re-identification key local, and generating the per-file Safe Harbor worksheet and residual-risk report that a data-sharing plan actually requires.
product_form: Browser-resident app with local WebGPU/WASM inference. UX: drop a folder; the app OCRs scans locally, runs a fine-tuned clinical de-identification token classifier over every document and column, and shows a reviewer queue where each detected identifier is highlighted in context with its class and confidence, surrogate value, and an accept/reject control. Output: de-identified copies written back to a folder the user chooses, an encrypted local surrogate map, and a generated evidence pack — which of the 18 Safe Harbor identifier classes were found and removed per file, what was left, and where the model was unsure.
ai_core: A fine-tuned specialized model, not a frontier API — because the input is PHI and cannot lawfully leave the machine without a BAA the buyer does not have. Base: a ModernBERT/DeBERTa-v3-small-class encoder (~140-180M params) exported to ONNX int8, run through transformers.js with `device: 'webgpu'` (HF docs, fetched 2026-08-20), plus a SmolDocling-256M-class VLM for scanned-document OCR and a deterministic rule layer for the structured identifiers (MRN patterns, dates, ZIP-to-three-digit truncation, ages over 89). Dataset assembled autonomously and licence-cleanly: generate a large synthetic clinical-narrative corpus with a frontier model (discharge summaries, progress notes, pathology reports, referral letters across specialties), then programmatically inject surrogate identifiers from public name/place/date generators — ground truth exists by construction, so labels cost nothing and there is no human annotation and no DUA. Target 500k-2M labelled spans. Public challenge corpora (i2b2/n2c2 2014 de-identification, 1,304 records, 28,872 PHI tokens) are used for external evaluation only where the data use agreement permits, and never as a commercial training dependency.
why_now: (a) Encoder-scale NER at 150M params quantised to int8 now runs at hundreds of tokens/second in a browser tab on integrated graphics — WebGPU is at 85.56% global support on July 2026 usage data (caniuse, fetched 2026-08-20) and transformers.js makes it a one-line device switch. (b) Sub-400M document VLMs that genuinely OCR scanned clinical paperwork in-browser shipped in 2025-2026 (SmolDocling-256M WebGPU). (c) Demand became mandatory: the NIH Data Management and Sharing Policy applies to all NIH-funded research generating scientific data from 25 January 2023, almost every competing award now needs an approved sharing plan, and NIH explicitly lists de-identification as an allowable cost — i.e. there is grant money earmarked for exactly this task. None of this was possible in 2022: the model quality was in the cloud, and the cloud is where PHI may not go.
buyer: NIH-funded academic research teams and core facilities preparing datasets for the sharing their DMS plan committed to; small CROs and site networks; digital-health and clinical-AI startups preparing training corpora; health-system innovation and quality groups. The defining trait is the same in every case: they hold PHI, they have no BAA with any AI vendor, they cannot install a Python pipeline on a locked-down institutional laptop, and they have a few hundred to a few thousand dollars of grant or project money — not the $20k-35k/yr an enterprise platform costs. Reachable self-serve: this cohort buys software on institutional cards and PIs choose their own tools.
market_evidence: (1) Tonic Textual — the closest commercial product for unstructured PHI de-identification — is quoted at roughly $20,000-35,000 per year for moderate volumes (Vendr marketplace/Codeables pricing analyses, surfaced 2026-08-20). That is the enterprise floor, and it prices out every lab. (2) HIPAA Expert Determination engagements run 'from a few thousand to tens of thousands of dollars' per project (Limina HIPAA expert determination cost guide, 2026-08-20) — direct evidence that money changes hands for the de-identification decision itself. (3) AWS Comprehend Medical sells a PHI Detection API metered in units of 100 characters with a 1-unit minimum per request (AWS pricing page, fetched 2026-08-20) — a per-character cloud meter on exactly this task. (4) NIH's DMS policy makes de-identification an allowable, budgeted cost line on almost every competing award since 25 Jan 2023. The gap is unmistakable: between a free Python library and a $20k/yr enterprise platform there is nothing a postdoc can buy on Tuesday.
incumbents: (1) **Microsoft Presidio** — free, MIT-licensed, 8,800+ GitHub stars, active releases through March 2026, with Analyzer/Anonymizer, an Image Redactor covering DICOM and OCR text, and structured-data support. This is the hardest competitor and the honest answer is that it sets the price floor at zero for anyone who can write Python. The gap: it is an SDK, not a product — no reviewer UI, no evidence pack, no browser delivery, and its default recognisers are general-purpose PII rather than clinical-narrative-tuned, which is where recall on real notes falls down. (2) **Tonic Textual** — purpose-built unstructured PHI de-identification with optional HIPAA Expert Determination, ~$20-35k/yr; enterprise procurement, sales-led. (3) **AWS Comprehend Medical PHI Detection** — tags the 18 Safe Harbor fields, metered per 100 characters, requires sending PHI to AWS under a BAA and requires an engineer to wire up. (4) **John Snow Labs de-identification** — high-quality clinical NLP, enterprise licensed, Spark/Python deployment. (5) **Datavant / Privacy Analytics (IQVIA)** — expert-determination and de-identification services, priced as engagements in the thousands-to-tens-of-thousands. Nobody in this list ships a zero-install, zero-upload, per-lab-priced tool. Note also, from this cycle's saturation sweep, that free browser-local tools have already colonised the *consumer-shaped* local-AI niches (video face blurring, bank-statement parsing) — they have not colonised this one, because the buyer needs an evidence artifact and a benchmark, not a toy.
moat: The fine-tune plus the eval harness, and the fact that both are publishable. Concretely: (a) a synthetically generated, fully-labelled clinical corpus that we own outright and can regenerate and expand by code — no DUA, no annotators, no licence encumbrance; (b) a clinical-narrative-tuned detector whose advantage over Presidio's general recognisers and over a frontier generalist is measured, not asserted, per identifier class (names in signature blocks, dates in narrative prose, provider vs patient name disambiguation, MRNs embedded in free text, ages over 89); (c) a versioned eval harness that ships a per-release scorecard — recall by identifier class on held-out data — attached to every evidence pack the customer generates. A researcher who must defend a data-sharing decision to an IRB needs a citable number; a chat assistant structurally cannot supply one. (d) Workflow depth: the surrogate map, the consistent pseudonymisation across a whole corpus, and the generated Safe Harbor worksheet are the parts a library does not give you.
inference_economics: Zero marginal cost — a ~150M int8 encoder plus a ~350M VLM run entirely on the customer's GPU; our variable cost is one-time model-bundle egress of roughly 250-600MB, about $0.02-0.05 per install, plus Stripe fees. At $99/month that is ~100% gross margin, invariant to how many notes the customer processes — which lets us sell unlimited volume against a competitor metering per 100 characters (AWS) or per document volume band (Tonic). Privacy is not a feature we bolt on; it is a consequence of the architecture, and it removes the BAA negotiation that is the single biggest friction in this buyer's purchase.
autonomy_case: A1: Stripe checkout, instant key, runs in the tab — no install, which matters because institutional laptops are locked down. A2: the de-identification, the surrogate mapping and the evidence pack are generated by code. A3 is the critical gate, because a false negative here is a PHI disclosure. Safeharbor never certifies that a file is de-identified and never uses the word 'compliant' about an output. It reports what it removed, per Safe Harbor identifier class, with per-span confidence, and it forces every below-threshold span into a mandatory review queue that must be cleared before export — the export is blocked, not warned about. Documents it cannot parse are listed in an explicit 'not analysed' appendix. The evidence pack states in fixed language that Safe Harbor requires removal of all 18 identifier classes and that the determination of adequacy rests with the covered entity or its expert, that this is tooling and not an Expert Determination under 45 CFR 164.514(b)(1), and it prints the model version and its published recall scorecard so the reader can judge. Self-serve refund: the customer can run our labelled synthetic validation set locally; if measured recall on their own machine falls below the published figure, the app triggers an automatic Stripe refund with no human contact. A4: the 18-identifier definition, ZIP-code population thresholds and geographic rules come from published HHS guidance refreshed on a schedule; the training corpus regenerates by code. A5/A6: no per-customer infrastructure exists — the compute is the customer's laptop.
pricing_hypothesis: Free tier: 20 pages, no signup, fully in-browser — the trust wedge, since this buyer will never upload a first test file to an unknown vendor. Lab tier $99/month or $890/year: unlimited documents, one workstation, evidence pack, surrogate map. Study tier $249/month: multiple workstations, consistent cross-corpus pseudonymisation, batch CSV/structured support. One-off 'Study Package' at $1,500 for a single dataset preparation — sized to sit inside the de-identification line item NIH already allows on the grant, and an order of magnitude under both an expert determination and Tonic's floor.
distribution: (1) SEO/answer-engine surface on the queries this buyer types: 'HIPAA Safe Harbor 18 identifiers', 'de-identify clinical notes', 'NIH DMS plan de-identification', 'Safe Harbor vs expert determination' — each landing on the free in-browser tool rather than a form. (2) The free tier is the channel: zero upload means a researcher can try it with a real note without an IRB conversation, which no cloud competitor can offer. (3) Publish the eval scorecard and the synthetic-corpus methodology as open artifacts — research buyers discover tools through methods write-ups and preprints, and this is content the incumbents do not publish at this price point. (4) University research-data-management LibGuides and core-facility tool lists (already dense with NIH DMS pages) are link targets reachable by writing something worth linking to. AP1 addressed: ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini at $0-20/mo cannot serve this user because the input is PHI without a BAA, because the job is a folder of 4,000 notes with consistent pseudonyms rather than one paste, and because the output must be a structured evidence artifact with a citable recall figure — vertical eval quality a generalist chat cannot certify. AP2 addressed: this is not 'summarise this page'. The browser's built-in AI is a cloud call on the current tab; here nothing may reach a cloud, and the unit of work is a directory, not a document.
risks: AP6 and honest unknowns. (1) **Presidio is free, MIT and backed by Microsoft** — the single largest risk. If Microsoft ships a polished browser build with a clinical model, the wedge narrows to the evidence pack and the UI. Our defence is the fine-tune plus the published harness, which is a maintained asset rather than a feature. (2) Licence risk on evaluation data: n2c2/i2b2 corpora are DUA-gated and their terms may bar commercial use — hence training on owned synthetic data and treating public corpora as evaluation-only-if-permitted. Unresolved until the DUA text is read. (3) Synthetic training data may not capture the messiness of real notes (transcription errors, abbreviations, scanned faxes); recall on real-world text is the central unproven claim. (4) Buyers may still need an Expert Determination for anything beyond Safe Harbor, capping our share of the job. (5) Browser platform: Chromium-only directory access (MDN lists showDirectoryPicker as limited-availability/experimental), and large corpora will hit memory ceilings without careful streaming. (6) Institutional buyers may demand a vendor security review even for a tool that transmits nothing, reintroducing human minutes — mitigation is a standing, generated security statement, but this is unproven. (7) NOT PROVEN: that a PI will pay $99/mo rather than assign a grad student and Presidio, and that our recall genuinely beats Presidio's clinical performance by a margin worth the money.

name: Adverse
one_liner: A conflicts-of-interest screening engine for small and mid-size law firms that builds the firm's adverse-party graph out of its own documents — not just what someone remembered to type into a form — and screens every new matter against it with cited evidence and a measured recall number.
product_form: Standalone web app (with an optional local indexing agent for firms that won't send documents to a cloud). UX: connect Clio / MyCase / PracticePanther and/or the firm's Dropbox/OneDrive/Google Drive matter folders; Adverse batch-indexes the historical corpus once (captions, engagement letters, contracts, correspondence, closing binders) into an entity graph of every party, counterparty, guarantor, insurer, principal and corporate parent it can find, each anchored to the document and page it came from. Then, on intake, you paste or type the new matter's parties and get a ranked hit list — each hit showing the matched entity, the source document quote, the relationship theory ("same person: middle initial + address match", "parent of your 2019 defendant per SEC EX-21"), and a confidence, which the lawyer clears or escalates in-product; the cleared record becomes the firm's audit trail.
ai_core: Two stages, deliberately split by cost. (1) EXTRACTION — a fine-tuned specialized model, not a frontier call, because this runs over tens of thousands of pages per firm. Base: an open 4–8B instruct model (Qwen3/Llama-class) served on our own GPUs or, for the privacy tier, on-device. Dataset we can assemble WITHOUT human labeling: CourtListener/RECAP bulk data is public domain, regenerated quarterly, and ships dockets with structured case metadata and party/attorney records (verified today at wiki.free.law) — the structured party table IS the label for the caption/document text, giving on the order of 10^5–10^6 auto-labeled (document text → party set with roles) examples for free; add SEC EX-21 subsidiary exhibits and Rule 7.1 corporate-disclosure statements for parent/subsidiary edges, and public bar/company registries for alias forms. Target: ~300k training pairs, zero human annotation. (2) ADJUDICATION — cheap blocking (embeddings + phonetic/edit-distance keys) narrows to ~10–30 candidates per query party, then a frontier call (Claude Haiku 4.5 at $1/$5 per MTok, or Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite at $0.10/$0.40, both fetched today) writes the same-entity judgment, the relationship theory, and the confidence, citing the source document. The frontier model never scans the corpus; it only argues about candidates the fine-tune surfaced.
why_now: Impossible before ~2023 for two reasons, both dated. (a) The firm's conflict history is not in a database — it is in scanned PDFs, DOCX engagement letters and email; extracting a structured party set from arbitrary legal documents at scale required vision-language document understanding, not OCR + regex. (b) Economics: indexing 50,000 pages (~50M tokens) is ~$2.50 of input at Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite batch pricing ($0.05/MTok input, $0.20/MTok output — ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing, fetched 2026-08-20) and ~$25 at Claude Haiku 4.5 batch ($0.50/$2.50 — platform.claude.com pricing, fetched 2026-08-20). In 2022 that same corpus pass was priced out of a $99/mo product by two orders of magnitude. That cost floor is exactly why every existing conflicts product is either an enterprise implementation (Intapp) or a manual-typing database (clientconflictcheck.com).
buyer: US law firms. ~463,600 law firms in the US as of 2024, with solo practices ~40% of firms and firms under six attorneys >75% of the total (Embroker's compilation of ABA/BLS data, fetched 2026-08-20). This is the exact segment that buys practice software self-serve with a credit card — Clio's entire business is evidence of that motion. Primary buyer: the 2–20 attorney firm and the small-firm office manager, where conflicts screening is done today by Ctrl-F in a spreadsheet or a single-term search in the practice management system. Secondary: small accounting/consulting firms with the same independence-check problem.
market_evidence: Money and losses already attach to this job. (1) Texas Lawyers' Insurance Exchange claims data: 16.4% of all claims reflected an allegation of conflict of interest, and 22.5% of all losses and defense costs involved a conflict of interest (TLIE data cited in Texas A&M law scholarship, fetched 2026-08-20) — the downstream cost is a malpractice claim, which is why LPL insurers publish conflict-avoidance guidance. (2) Firms already pay cash for a far weaker product: clientconflictcheck.com sells a hosted conflicts database at $199/year (solo) and $249/year (mid-size) (pricing page fetched 2026-08-20) — but it only searches names a human typed in, so it cannot catch a party buried in a 2019 settlement agreement. (3) At the top end, Intapp sells Conflicts to law, accounting, consulting, investment banking and private capital firms entirely sales-led with no public price (intapp.com/risk/conflicts, fetched 2026-08-20). The middle — a firm with 40,000 documents and no $50k budget — is unserved.
incumbents: Five closest, each checked live today. (1) Intapp Conflicts — enterprise entity resolution for conflicts; no public pricing, every CTA is 'Schedule a demo' (intapp.com/risk/conflicts, fetched 2026-08-20). Gap: sales-led, priced for AmLaw/large accounting, not reachable self-serve. (2) Clio's built-in Conflict Check — Clio's own help center documents the ceiling: Global Search/Conflict Check 'will only search for one item at a time' with a workaround of up to ten individual searches before generating results, and the mode is Flex vs Exact string matching over Clio records only; a Grow check does not check Manage at the same time (support.clio.com / help.clio.com articles, retrieved 2026-08-20; help.clio.com returns HTTP 403 to automated fetch). Gap: string search over structured fields — no extraction from documents, no corporate-family reasoning, no ranked evidence. (3) Lawmatics — intake CRM; conflict checking included in all tiers ('basic' on Essential, 'advanced' on Premium/Enterprise), 3-user minimum, no dollar figures published, every CTA is 'Get a demo'/'Contact Sales' (lawmatics.com/pricing, fetched 2026-08-20). Gap: conflicts over CRM contact records the firm typed in. (4) clientconflictcheck.com — $199/yr solo, $249/yr mid-size, large firms custom (pricing.html, fetched 2026-08-20); describes type-ahead search and claims no fuzzy, phonetic or AI matching anywhere. Gap: manual-entry index; garbage-in is the whole failure mode. (5) Smokeball — practice management with basic conflict screening bundled, the low-cost entry option. Gap: same string-match-on-entered-data shape. DUE-DILIGENCE NOTE: several 2026 'best conflict check software' comparison pages (ustechautomations.com, krowdbase.com, caseledge.com, aivortex.io) name AI-native conflicts vendors including 'DeepKnit' and 'Vida.io'. I checked: deepknit.ai resolves (HTTP 200) but is a general 'AI workflow automation platform' for document processing across healthcare/insurance/legal, demo-led, with no conflicts product (fetched 2026-08-20). Those pages are SEO content farms and are not evidence of a competitor. No verified self-serve, document-derived conflicts product exists today.
moat: Three layers, and the fine-tune is load-bearing. (a) ASSEMBLED DATASET → FINE-TUNE: RECAP/CourtListener bulk data is public domain and quarterly-refreshed, and its structured docket party/attorney tables auto-label the unstructured caption and filing text — ~300k (document → party set with roles) training pairs and an alias corpus with zero human annotation, plus corporate-family edges from SEC EX-21 exhibits and Rule 7.1 disclosures. A frontier generalist is fine at 'is Jon Smith John Smyth?' but has never been optimized for exhaustive party recall across a 90-page scanned settlement agreement, and cannot be certified on it. (b) EVAL HARNESS: held-out dockets give ground-truth party sets, so we publish a measured per-entity-type precision AND recall figure, refreshed each quarter as new bulk data lands. Recall is the number a law firm actually needs and the number no chat assistant can produce; selling a certified recall figure is the product. (c) USAGE-ACCUMULATED: each firm's entity graph — every alias, every cleared/escalated decision, every 'this Acme is not that Acme' — deepens monthly and is worthless to a competitor. Switching cost is the audit trail itself.
inference_economics: One-time index: a 5-attorney firm with ~50,000 pages ≈ 50M input tokens. At Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite batch ($0.05/MTok in, $0.20/MTok out, fetched today) that is ~$2.50 input plus ~$2–4 of structured output — call it $5–10; at Claude Haiku 4.5 batch ($0.50/$2.50) ~$25–40. Budget $15–50 one-time per firm, amortized over 12 months. Steady state: a new matter with 4 query parties × ~25 adjudications × ~3k tokens ≈ 300k tokens ≈ $0.03 at Flash-Lite, $0.30 at Haiku 4.5; 30 matters/month costs $1–9/month against a $149–249/month price. Gross margin >95%. LOCAL OPTION: the extraction fine-tune is 4–8B and can run on-device (WebGPU/Ollama) for a 'documents never leave the firm' tier — zero marginal inference cost and privacy by construction, the objection that kills cloud tools in this segment.
autonomy_case: A1 self-serve: card, OAuth into Clio/Drive, index runs unattended — the same motion as every practice-management add-on. A2 fulfilment is entirely code. A3 DEGRADATION IS THE CORE DESIGN, not a bolt-on: Adverse is a SCREENING tool and never issues a clearance. It returns ranked candidate hits, each with source document, quoted line, relationship theory and calibrated confidence; the lawyer adjudicates in-product and their decision — not ours — is the record. Wrong output degrades asymmetrically: a false positive costs 15 seconds of reading, and false negatives are attacked structurally (published recall from the held-out eval, a nightly second-pass sweep at a lower threshold that re-opens matters when new hits appear, and an explicit 'documents we could not read' list so the firm knows the coverage boundary). We never sell the unverifiable assertion 'you are clear'. A4: RECAP bulk regenerates quarterly and SEC EX-21 filings arrive continuously; both ingest on a cron. A5/A6: no onboarding call, no implementation, no human minutes — the firm's own document store is the configuration.
pricing_hypothesis: $99/mo solo, $249/mo for 2–10 attorneys, $499/mo for 11–30, plus a one-time $199–499 corpus indexing fee for backfiles over 100k pages (covers the batch inference and prepays cost-to-serve). Local/on-prem privacy tier at +$100/mo. Free wedge: index up to 2,000 documents and run 5 screens free — enough that the first run surfaces a party the firm did not know it had. Anchors: clientconflictcheck.com at $199–249/YEAR is the floor for 'a place to type names'; Intapp is the ceiling; the value anchor is TLIE's 22.5%-of-losses figure.
distribution: All zero-human. (1) Clio App Directory + MyCase/PracticePanther marketplaces — the canonical install surface for this buyer; a listing is a store page, not a sales call. (2) SEO/AEO on high-intent queries the content farms currently own with garbage ('how to run a conflict check', 'conflict check software for solo firm', 'what if I missed a conflict'). (3) A free public utility: paste a case caption, get the extracted party set and corporate family — a shareable demo of the extraction model costing fractions of a cent. (4) State bar practice-management advisor listings and LPL insurer risk-management resource pages, which routinely list conflict-system vendors. (5) r/LawFirm, solo/small-firm groups, ABA Solo & Small Firm TechReport readership. AP1 ANSWER: the corpus is confidential, 10–100GB, and the job is RECALL-critical over the firm's private history — ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini at $20/mo cannot index it, cannot be pointed at Clio's document store, and cannot certify a recall number the firm can show its malpractice carrier. Batch scale (tens of thousands of documents), embedded at the exact point of work (intake), producing a structured audit record. AP2 ANSWER: the opposite of 'summarize this page' — there is no page; the artifact is a persistent private entity graph plus a decision log, which an agentic browser has no path to build or maintain.

name: PremiumDiff
one_liner: Upload this month's carrier benefit invoices and your enrollment census; get back, in minutes, every employee you're being billed for who left, every one who's missing, every wrong tier and rate — each finding pinned to the invoice line it came from with a dollar figure and a ready-to-send dispute packet.
product_form: Standalone web app, no integration required to get value. UX: drag in the carrier invoice PDFs/CSVs (medical, dental, vision, life — typically 5–12 files, some 200 pages of member-level lines) and a census export from the ben-admin/HRIS/payroll system; PremiumDiff parses every invoice into member-level rows, resolves each row to a census person, and returns a reconciliation split into auto-cleared / discrepancy / needs-your-eyes — each with the cropped invoice line, the census row, the dollar delta and a confidence. Second screen: a per-carrier dispute packet (PDF + CSV) you email the carrier, plus a month-over-month ledger tracking retro credits to resolution.
ai_core: Two stages. (1) PARSING — a frontier vision-language call over each invoice page (Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite or Claude Haiku 4.5 as workhorse, Claude Sonnet 5 for pages the cheap model flags low-confidence) turning arbitrary carrier layouts into member-level structured rows: name, member ID, plan, tier, coverage period, rate, premium, adjustments. No templates — that is the entire point. (2) MATCHING — a fine-tuned specialized model, because this is where generalists fumble: resolving invoice person → census person across nicknames (Bob/Robert), maiden/married names, transposed or truncated names, dependents billed under a subscriber, and member IDs that differ per carrier; plus tier normalization ('EE+SP' / 'Employee + Spouse' / '2-Party' / 'Two Party' are one thing, 'EE+1' is not always). Base: a 1–4B embedding + cross-encoder pair (embeddings for blocking, cross-encoder for the match decision) fine-tuned on a corpus we assemble autonomously: (a) synthetic pair generation — public SHOP/exchange plan documents and rate sheets crossed with generated census populations, programmatically corrupted along the real failure axes (nickname substitution, name truncation, tier-label variance, dependent rollup, mid-month proration), yielding 10^5–10^6 labeled pairs with no human annotation; (b) every customer correction in the 'needs your eyes' queue is a free gold label produced by the customer's own work, not our labor. The frontier model writes the human-readable discrepancy explanation and adjudicates residual ambiguous pairs.
why_now: Two dated capabilities. (a) Carrier premium invoices arrive in hundreds of distinct layouts, many scanned or generated PDFs with hundreds of member lines; before vision-language document understanding (~2023 onward) reading them required per-carrier template engineering — which is precisely why every incumbent here is an implementation-and-services business rather than a product you buy with a card. Beneration's VerifiaBill, the 'affordable' option, still states reports are delivered within 5 business days after all invoices are received (beneration.com, fetched 2026-08-20): that latency is a human doing the reading. (b) Cost: a 150-page invoice at ~1,500 tokens/page is ~225k input tokens ≈ $0.011 at Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite batch pricing ($0.05/MTok in, fetched 2026-08-20). In 2022, template-free parsing at that price did not exist at any quality.
buyer: Two adjacent self-serve buyers. (1) Employers with roughly 20–500 employees — Census Business Dynamics Statistics counts ~5.52 million US firms with 1–499 employees (2022, up from 5.38M in 2021, census.gov small-business resources, fetched 2026-08-20); the 20–500 slice is where group benefits exist, an HR generalist owns the invoice, and there is no benefits-billing department. This buyer is explicitly under the floor of the market leader: Tabulera's Starter plan is $399/mo ($319/mo annual) for companies under 500 employees, and it is still demo-led. (2) Small benefits brokers and agencies running 20–80 client groups, who do this reconciliation as an unbilled retention service in Excel — they buy per-group and are reachable through broker communities. inference_economics: Per invoice: ~150 pages × ~1,500 tokens = ~225k input tokens. Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite batch ($0.05/MTok in, $0.20/MTok out, fetched today): ~$0.011 input + ~$0.02 structured output ≈ $0.03. Claude Haiku 4.5 batch ($0.50/$2.50): ~$0.11 + ~$0.25 ≈ $0.36. Escalating ~10% of low-confidence pages to Claude Sonnet 5 ($2/$10 standard) adds ~$0.10. Matching: the cross-encoder is ours (near-zero marginal cost); frontier adjudication of ~100 ambiguous pairs × 2k tokens ≈ 200k tokens ≈ $0.01–0.20. A customer with 6 carriers costs roughly $0.20–$3.00/month of inference against a $99–199/month price → 97–99% gross margin, with headroom to run every job twice (cheap pass + verification pass) and still clear 95%. Prompt caching on the census side (cache reads at 0.1x input) makes re-runs and month-over-month comparisons nearly free. Local/WebGPU is NOT the wedge here — parsing needs a real VLM — so the privacy answer is zero-retention API configuration plus a click-through BAA, not on-device inference.
autonomy_case: A1: card, upload, result — no demo, which is the entire competitive thesis given all five incumbents are demo-led. A2: fulfilment is a batch pipeline. A3 DEGRADATION: every finding is evidence-anchored — cropped invoice line, census row, computed delta, calibrated confidence — and findings below threshold go into a separate 'needs your eyes' queue EXCLUDED from the headline recovery total, so we never sell an unverifiable dollar figure. Pages the parser could not read are listed explicitly as coverage gaps rather than silently dropped. Money-back on month one if the audit surfaces nothing (cheap: inference is cents). A4: carrier layout profiles self-maintain from traffic; plan/rate reference data is re-derived from the customer's own uploads each month, so nothing goes stale. A5: unattended batch. name: Walkcode
one_liner: Narrate a housing unit walkthrough into your phone's browser; get back every observation coded to the exact HUD NSPIRE standard, severity tier and correction deadline — with the audio span behind each line and nothing invented.
product_form: Browser-resident PWA (no app store). The inspector/maintenance lead opens walkcode.app on a phone, hits record, and talks their way through a unit; audio and photos buffer in IndexedDB and sync when signal returns. Output is a per-unit deficiency record (CSV/JSON/PDF) where each row is {spoken span → NSPIRE standard id → inspectable area → severity → correction timeframe → confidence}, plus a fix-first punch list ordered by severity; a WebGPU 'local mode' toggle runs Whisper-turbo + the classifier entirely on-device so no unit audio leaves the phone.
ai_core: Three-stage, deliberately NOT one frontier prompt. (1) ASR: Whisper-large-v3-turbo via transformers.js/WebGPU on-device by default; Deepgram Nova-3 pre-recorded ($0.0043/min, fetched today) as the cloud fallback for weak devices. (2) The actual product: a FINE-TUNED specialized classifier mapping a colloquial maintenance utterance ('the GFCI in the back bath won't trip', 'no smoke alarm in the rear bedroom', 'handrail's loose on the basement stairs') to {NSPIRE standard id, inspectable area, severity tier, correction timeframe}. Base model: a small encoder/decoder that quantizes into the browser — DistilBERT-class encoder for the retrieval head plus a Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B-class generator for severity+rationale. Dataset we assemble autonomously: HUD publishes all 71 NSPIRE standards as individual PDFs plus a one-click .ZIP (7MB) and a changelogs PDF (2.4MB) (fetched hud.gov/reac/nspire-standards today); each standard enumerates deficiency criteria and severity by inspectable area, giving several hundred canonical rows whose LABEL IS THE SOURCE DOCUMENT — zero human labeling. We then generate 30–50k training pairs by conditioning Claude Sonnet 5 on each labeled criterion to emit 15–25 colloquial/field paraphrases (English + Spanish, including tech shorthand and mis-hearings), plus in-product user corrections as the ongoing signal. (3) A frontier call (Claude Sonnet 5, $2/$10 per MTok fetched today) is used ONLY to segment continuous narration into discrete observations and to draft the correction punch list — never to assert a code and never to invent an observation.
why_now: Two things, both dated. Capability: browser-local speech recognition good enough for noisy on-site narration plus in-browser WebGPU inference of a fine-tuned classifier — impossible pre-2023 (Whisper released Sept 2022; WebGPU shipped in Chrome 113, May 2023). Regulatory: NSPIRE itself is new — HUD's final standards were published 22 June 2023 and the individual standard documents are dated 11 Aug 2023 (fetched hud.gov/reac/nspire-standards, 2026-08-20). The voucher-side compliance date was extended a third time, to 1 Feb 2027, by Federal Register notice published 30 Sept 2025 (fetched today). So there is a live, dated, forced migration off HQS with an installed base that has never used this taxonomy.
buyer: Three self-serve segments, in order of pain. (a) Independent/contract housing inspectors: PHAs outsource NSPIRE inspection work to vendors whose field inspectors do 8–15 units/day and write them up after hours. (b) Small-to-mid property management companies and affordable-housing maintenance supervisors doing pre-inspection walks before a REAC/NSPIRE visit — a 200-unit property is 2,000+ observations in a week. (c) HCV/PBV landlords who lose HAP payments while a failed unit waits on re-inspection. BLS sizes the adjacent inspector labor pool at 365,300 for claims adjusters/appraisers/examiners/investigators (2024, fetched bls.gov today) — Walkcode targets the housing-inspection slice plus PM firms, not that whole number. Honest sourcing gap: I could not fetch a primary count of NSPIRE contract inspectors; the PHA count (~3,000+) and Gilson's per-unit pricing calculator (fetched today) imply the buying unit is 'per portfolio', which is why the wedge is the individual inspector seat, not a PHA procurement.

Gilson Housing Partners sells the iNSPIRE app to Housing Authorities with a quote-based per-unit pricing calculator (fetched today). inference_economics: Per unit inspected (~8–12 min of narration, 10–25 observations). Cloud path: Deepgram Nova-3 pre-recorded at $0.0043/min = $0.043 (fetched today); alternative gpt-4o-mini-transcribe $0.003/min = $0.030 or gpt-transcribe $0.0045/min (fetched developers.openai.com today); segmentation + punch-list on Claude Haiku 4.5 at $1/$5 per MTok with the taxonomy prompt-cached (cache read 0.1x = $0.10/MTok) → ~6k cached input + 1.5k output ≈ $0.008. Total cloud ≈ $0.05/unit. Local path (default): Whisper-turbo + quantized classifier on WebGPU = $0.00 marginal, and the audio never leaves the device — which is the actual sales line to a PM firm holding tenant-identifiable audio. At $49/mo for 60 units the cloud-path COGS is $3.00 against $49 (94% gross margin); local mode makes it ~100% minus hosting.
autonomy_case: A1 self-serve: card checkout, free tier of 5 units/month, no demo (the two closest housing incumbents are quote-gated — that is the wedge, not an accident). A3 degradation, the core of the design: (i) every coded row renders the verbatim HUD standard text beside it and links back to the audio span, so the user is never asked to trust an unsourced assertion; (ii) an utterance the classifier cannot place above threshold becomes 'Uncoded observation — review', never a guessed standard; (iii) the product never emits 'this unit passes' — it emits 'N observations map to Life-Threatening under Standard X', which is a sourced claim, not an unverifiable one; (iv) if HUD's changelog moves a standard after the walk, affected rows auto-flag for re-review; (v) automatic refund on any report where >20% of observations came back uncoded. A4: the reference data self-maintains — HUD publishes the 71 standards plus a changelogs PDF; a weekly job re-downloads the ZIP, diffs it, re-parses, re-runs the eval harness and only promotes the new taxonomy if accuracy holds. (1) SEO on the long tail of the taxonomy itself: 'is a missing GFCI life-threatening under NSPIRE', 'NSPIRE correction timeframe smoke alarm' — thousands of queries generated from the 71 parsed standards, each landing on a free public deficiency-lookup page. That lookup is the marketing surface and the free-tier wedge; the paid product is the audio→coded record, so this is not a knowledge-base product. (1) The assembled dataset: HUD's 71 standards parsed into a structured deficiency taxonomy (severity tier + correction timeframe + inspectable area per criterion), auto-diffed against HUD's own changelog — nobody has published this as machine-readable, and building it is a real parsing job, not a prompt. (2) The fine-tuned classifier trained on 30–50k label-conditioned paraphrase pairs generated from that taxonomy plus accumulating in-product corrections; this beats a frontier generalist on the task for the same reason a specialist beats a generalist anywhere — the generalist has to be told 400 deficiency criteria in-context every call, degrades on colloquial trade phrasing and Spanish, and has no calibrated abstain behaviour. (3) The eval harness that proves it: a held-out benchmark of real field phrasings with per-standard top-1 accuracy, severity accuracy, and — the number that matters commercially — abstain-precision (of the items we DID code, what fraction a certified inspector agrees with). We publish it. That published number is the thing a chat assistant structurally cannot offer and the thing a compliance buyer needs. Usage compounds it: every correction is a labeled example.
risks: AP6 platform risk: HUD has now extended the voucher compliance date three times (to 1 Feb 2027, Federal Register 30 Sept 2025, fetched today) — a fourth slip would delay the HCV segment, though public housing and HUD multifamily are already inspected under NSPIRE, so the inspector/PM segments exist regardless; I did not independently fetch a primary source for those earlier effective dates, so treat that as an inference from the notice's scope. HUD could publish its own mapping tool or a machine-readable taxonomy, which would erase moat layer (1) but not (2) or (3). Model risk is low (multi-vendor ASR, and local mode removes API dependency entirely); no app-store policy exposure since it is a PWA. Competitive risk: ReportWalk or Property Inspect adding an NSPIRE pack — mitigated only by the eval harness and the correction corpus, i.e. we must ship the benchmark early and loudly. NOT YET PROVEN: (i) that independent NSPIRE inspectors will pay $49/mo out of pocket rather than use employer-mandated software — this is the single riskiest assumption and needs 20 cold conversations or a landing-page test before any build; (ii) the size of the contract-inspector population (no primary source found); (iii) that a browser-quantized classifier hits acceptable top-1 accuracy on the 71-standard taxonomy — the cloud path is the fallback and the local path is the differentiator, so a failed WebGPU eval costs the privacy wedge, not the product.
