name: Chattel
one_liner: Executors photograph a deceased person's home; Chattel returns an itemised, room-by-room contents schedule where every line carries real auction/resale comparables with dates and links — the evidence pack behind the s.160 IHTA 1984 open-market figure on IHT400, in minutes for £39 instead of £99+VAT and 1-3 days from a human valuer.
product_form: Standalone web app (no extension, no install). UX: (1) the executor walks the house with their phone, uploading 60-150 photos into room buckets from a browser page — no app store, no login wall until checkout; (2) minutes later they get a paginated PDF plus a CSV, one row per item, each with condition, quantity, a low-high open-market range, the 3-8 realised comparables that range was derived from (lot title, house, date, hammer), and a coverage flag; items with too few comparables are printed in a separate 'insufficient market evidence — obtain specialist valuation' schedule, excluded from the total and not billed.
ai_core: Two-stage, and only stage one is a frontier call. Stage 1 — extraction: Claude Sonnet 5 (claude-sonnet-5, $3/MTok in) over batched room photos returns a strict-schema JSON inventory (item, category, material, maker/marks read off the object, condition, quantity, room, source photo + bbox). Claude Opus 5 (claude-opus-5, $5/MTok in) is used only on items the first pass flags as high-value or ambiguous. Stage 2 — the specialised model we own: a fine-tuned image+text retrieval encoder (SigLIP-class / Qwen3-VL-class open weights) mapping a lot photo and its extracted description into a comparables index, plus a quantile-regression calibration head that turns the retrieved comparables into a low/high range with a coverage score. Dataset we assemble autonomously: (lot image, title, description, category, hammer price, sale date, house) tuples from publicly published auction results — LiveAuctioneers' free results database is 21M records back to 1999, updated daily (fetched today), the-saleroom publishes results openly for 5 days after each sale before they move behind the Price Guide paywall (fetched today), and individual auctioneers publish their own results pages. Target 500k-2M tuples for v1. The label is free and needs no annotator: the realised hammer price IS the ground truth, so labelling is fully autonomous. That is what makes a fine-tune rational here rather than decorative — a frontier generalist has no index of what a 1960s teak sideboard actually fetched in Shropshire last month, and cannot be made to have one by prompting.
why_now: Two dated capability shifts. (1) High-resolution vision: per Anthropic's vision docs fetched today, the high-resolution tier (2576 px long edge, up to 4784 visual tokens per image) exists only on 'Claude 4.7 and later models' — earlier models downscale to 1568 px / 1568 tokens. Reading a maker's mark, a silver hallmark, a back-stamp or a model number off an object sitting in a wide room photo is precisely what the extra ~3x visual-token budget buys; at 1568-token standard resolution that text is gone. (2) The same doc gives the cost: a 1000x1000 image is 1296 visual tokens, ~$6.48 per thousand images on Opus 5, ~$1.30 per thousand on Haiku 4.5 — so a 120-photo house costs cents, not dollars. Neither the fidelity nor the price existed before ~2023, and the fidelity specifically not before the 4.7-class models.
buyer: Primary: executors and administrators of UK estates. Volume is official and large — MoJ/HMCTS Family Court Statistics Quarterly (gov.uk, fetched today) records 65,099 probate applications and 64,595 grants issued in Jan-Mar 2025 alone, i.e. ~250-260k grants/year in England & Wales, with 93% of applications made digitally (so the buyer is already transacting online, unassisted). Secondary and more durable: the trade that currently outsources this — probate solicitors and will-writers, online probate providers, and house-clearance/estate-clearance firms who need a contents figure before quoting. Both are reachable self-serve: consumer by search, trade by an API key and a CSV.
market_evidence: Money is already changing hands for exactly this deliverable, at a published self-serve price, fulfilled by humans looking at customer-supplied photos. Swift Values sells an online house-contents probate valuation at £99 + VAT: the customer photographs the items and uploads them, a team assesses them remotely, and a PDF comes back in 1-3 working days containing a room-by-room illustrated record, a Section 160 IHTA 1984 compliance statement, a signed declaration for IHT400 and a valuer biography; individual item valuations are from £25 + VAT and in-person from £249 + VAT per hour (fetched today). Avery Associates sells the same document compiled by a RICS valuer, 5 working days standard, 24 hours urgent, price on application (fetched today). The workflow — customer takes the photos, a remote human turns them into a priced schedule — is already the market norm; the only human left in it is the pricing judgement, which is the part with a public ground-truth dataset. Swift Values also markets the demand driver: it claims 'over 80% of people overvalue household contents' and therefore overpay IHT (vendor claim, fetched today, not independently verified).
incumbents: (1) Swift Values — swiftvalues.co.uk, £99+VAT online photo-based probate contents valuation, £25+VAT per item, £249+VAT/hr in person, 1-3 working days, human-fulfilled, claims a 100% HMRC acceptance record with money back if rejected (fetched 2026-08-20). Gap: human throughput, 1-3 day turnaround, and no per-item comparable evidence shown to the customer. (2) Avery Associates — averyassociates.co.uk, RICS valuer compiles the IHT chattels valuation, 5 working days (24h urgent), fixed fee quoted privately (fetched 2026-08-20). Gap: no published price, no self-serve checkout, no evidence trail. (3) Appraizely — AI valuation 'backed by 5M+ auction records' across 870+ categories from 500+ houses, subscription for unlimited access, pricing page returned 404 today (page fetched 2026-08-20; /pricing 404 on 2026-08-20). Gap: it is a US-leaning collector research tool for single items — it does not produce a UK estate-level schedule, does not shape output to IHT400/s.160, and publishes no accuracy figure. (4) Mearto — online appraisals of fine art, antiques and collectibles by human specialists 'combining industry knowledge with online research data'; the page carries no price or turnaround (fetched 2026-08-20). Gap: per-item, human, art-and-antiques-only, not whole-house. (5) The US contents-inventory AI cohort — Scanlily ('record a video, AI returns an itemised inventory with RCV and comparable links'), My Property Vault ('photograph each room, AI builds a valued home inventory... for insurance, estate planning and divorce'), Club of Things, Insurnest's Contents Valuation AI Agent (search results, 2026-08-20). Gap: all are US insurance-replacement-cost engines. Replacement cost new is the wrong number for probate — HMRC wants open market value on the date of death under s.160 — and none of them cite UK realised auction prices or shape a s.160 schedule. The empty flank is precise: nobody sells a UK estate-scale, comparable-cited, open-market-value schedule instantly and self-serve. Chrome Web Store install counts are not relevant — this is not an extension, and nothing in this workflow lives in the browser chrome.
moat: Three layers, in increasing durability. (1) The comparables index: a continuously ingested corpus of publicly published realised prices, refreshed daily, mapped into a fine-tuned image+text embedding space. Building it is a months-long data-engineering job, not a prompt. (2) The eval harness, which is also the marketing: hold out recent sales and publish, live, three numbers — range-hit rate (did the actual hammer land inside our predicted low-high), median absolute percentage error, and coverage (share of items with ≥3 comparables). No incumbent publishes any accuracy figure; even the auction-tooling market's own buyer's guide (Gavelist, fetched today) warns that estimate 'quality varies widely' and tells auctioneers to test tools 'on items where you already know the answer'. Being the only party with a published, continuously re-measured number on that exact question is a defensible position, and it is the fine-tune's justification: a frontier generalist cannot be certified on this task because it has no retrieval basis and no held-out set. (3) Usage-accumulated outcome data: clearance firms and auctioneers who use the trade API later tell us what the items actually sold for. That closes a prediction→outcome loop a prose-generating competitor never sees, and it compounds per customer.
inference_economics: Per estate pack: ~120 room photos. At the documented ⌈w/28⌉×⌈h/28⌉ formula, a 1000x1000 photo is 1296 visual tokens, so 120 photos ≈ 156k visual tokens — $0.47 on Sonnet 5 ($3/MTok input) or $0.16 on Haiku 4.5 ($1/MTok, standard tier). The comparables-reasoning pass over ~200 extracted items at ~2k tokens of retrieved context each ≈ 400k tokens ≈ $1.20 on Sonnet 5. Opus 5 is called only on flagged items (typically <10 per estate) — the docs' own figure is ~$6.48 per thousand 1MP images at Opus 5 high-resolution. All-in ≈ $1.50-$3.50 per pack against a £39 price: ~90% gross margin with room to absorb a 3x cost regression. Stage 2 has no API cost at all — the retrieval encoder and calibration head are our own weights on our own GPU (and the encoder is small enough to be a candidate for client-side WebGPU later, which would also make the photos never leave the device — a genuine privacy claim for a product that photographs a dead person's home). Local-model option therefore exists for the half of the pipeline that runs most often.
autonomy_case: A1: upload, preview 10 items free, pay by card, download — no call, no demo, no account required before the preview. A2: the whole pipeline is code; the PDF/CSV is generated, not assembled by anyone. A3 is the design centre, because the output touches tax. The product never asserts a valuation. Every line prints its evidence: N comparables with lot title, auction house, sale date and hammer price, plus a low-high range and a coverage score. Below 3 comparables the item is moved to a separate 'insufficient market evidence' schedule, excluded from the estate total, explicitly flagged for a specialist, and not charged for. The cover page states plainly what the document is — an evidence pack supporting the executor's own open-market estimate under s.160 IHTA 1984 — and what it is not: a professional valuation, no RICS/SOFAA signature, no HMRC acceptance guarantee. Anything the extractor believes may exceed the ~£1,500 single-item level at which HMRC expects a formal professional valuation is auto-flagged rather than priced. Refund is automatic and code-issued if coverage falls below a published threshold. A4: the comparables index re-ingests daily and re-fits the calibration head weekly, unattended. A5/A6: no human touches a customer job, ever.
pricing_hypothesis: £39 per estate pack (undercuts the £99+VAT human service by ~60% and returns in minutes rather than 1-3 days). Free preview of the first 10 items to prove quality before payment. £12 per single deep-dive item (against £25+VAT). Trade tier for solicitors, online probate providers and clearance firms: £19/estate at 10+/month via API and CSV, so the professional can attach their own sign-off on top of our evidence — this is the tier that likely carries the business.
distribution: All zero-human channels. (1) Search: 'probate valuation house contents', 'do I need a valuation for probate', 'IHT400 household contents', 'section 160 open market value' — high, dated, non-recurring intent currently answered by £99+ human firms and by law-firm blog posts; we can outrank on a free calculator plus the schedule template. (2) A programmatically generated, self-maintaining public price index: one page per category ('what 1970s G Plan teak actually sells for, updated daily') built straight from the comparables index — an SEO surface that grows without anyone writing it, and simultaneously the public proof of the dataset. (3) Free-tier wedge: the 10-item preview is the whole demo. (4) Affiliate links (code-issued, no calls) from will-writers, online probate services and house-clearance firms. (5) Communities: r/UKPersonalFinance, r/LegalAdviceUK, MoneySavingExpert probate threads — dense, recurring, high-intent questions about exactly this. AP1 answered: this is 200+ items cross-referenced against a proprietary realised-price index and shaped into a tax-facing schedule with a published error rate — not one question to a chatbot. ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini at $20/mo have no UK realised-price index, cannot hold a consistent item taxonomy across 120 photos, cannot certify accuracy on this task, and will not print a per-line comparable trail. AP2 answered: nothing here is 'summarise or act on this page'. The input is a batch of camera-roll photos and the output is a downloadable document — Chrome's Gemini and agentic browsers have no surface on it.
risks: The central unproven thing, stated plainly: Swift Values' £99 does not buy labour, it buys a signature, a valuer biography and a money-back-if-HMRC-rejects guarantee. We cannot sell any of those three. It is genuinely unknown whether a nervous executor will choose an unsigned evidence pack at £39 over a signed one at £99 — and if they will not, the business is the trade tier (solicitors and clearance firms who supply their own sign-off over our evidence), which is still fully self-serve but a smaller, slower market. Second: legal/tax consequence. An under-stated contents figure exposes the executor to HMRC penalties; our mitigation is evidence-not-assertion, conservative ranges, the >£1,500 auto-flag and explicit non-valuation framing, but a regulator or a professional body could still take the view that the product strays toward reserved valuation work. Third, AP6 platform risk: model deprecation is low (extraction is model-agnostic and the moat is the index, not the prompt), but data-sourcing terms are a real medium-high risk — LiveAuctioneers' free results database and the-saleroom's 5-day public window are governed by site terms we have not audited, and a scraping block or a ToS action would hit the moat directly; the mitigation is to prioritise auctioneers' own published results, negotiate direct feeds, and lean on customer-supplied outcome data, none of which is proven yet. Fourth: one-shot buyer, no retention, so LTV is a single £39 and CAC on probate search terms is expensive — the self-maintaining price-index SEO surface has to work or the unit economics do not. Fifth: Appraizely already has 5M auction records and an AI estimate; if it turns UK-and-probate-shaped it becomes a direct competitor overnight.

name: Realised
one_liner: A per-item valuation layer for the second-hand trade whose product is a number you can defend, not prose: photos in, a low-high range out, every range grounded in retrieved realised hammer prices, with a live public scoreboard of our range-hit rate and median error against actual sales.
product_form: Standalone web app plus a batch API/CSV that clips onto the cataloguing tool the customer already uses. UX: an auctioneer or clearance firm drags in a folder of lot photos (1,000+ at a time) and gets back a CSV with one row per lot — predicted low/high, confidence, coverage, and the comparable lots behind it — importable into AuctionFlex, Proxibid, LiveAuctioneers or their existing cataloguer. The onboarding is the proof: upload 100 lots you have already sold, and before paying anything you see our error rate on your own past hammer prices.
ai_core: Deliberately not a frontier chat call at the point of value. A frontier model (Claude Sonnet 5, claude-sonnet-5) does one job — turning 2-4 photos per lot into a structured description: category, period, material, maker's marks and back-stamps read off the object, damage and restoration, dimensions cues. Claude Opus 5 (claude-opus-5) is reserved for lots the first pass flags as high-value or contradictory across photos. The valuation itself is a specialised model we own: a fine-tuned multimodal retrieval encoder (SigLIP-class or Qwen3-VL-class open weights) over a comparables index, plus a quantile-regression calibration head producing a low/high interval and a coverage score. Dataset assembled autonomously: (lot image, title, description, category, hammer price, sale date, house) tuples harvested from publicly published realised prices — LiveAuctioneers' free 21M-record database updated daily, the-saleroom's 5-day open results window, and auctioneers' own results pages. Target 500k-2M tuples at v1, growing daily. Labelling requires zero humans because the hammer price is the label. This is the whole argument for a fine-tune over a generalist: the task is retrieval-and-calibration against a market, and prompting cannot conjure a market.
why_now: Same dated capability as Chattel, plus an economic one. Anthropic's vision docs (fetched today) show the high-resolution tier — 2576 px long edge, up to 4784 visual tokens — is restricted to 'Claude 4.7 and later models'; below that, images downscale to 1568 px and the hallmark, signature, back-stamp or model number that determines a lot's value is unreadable. And the price makes per-lot inference viable: 1296 visual tokens for a 1MP image, ~$1.30 per thousand such images on Haiku 4.5, ~$6.48 on Opus 5. The market timing is the second half of it — a cataloguing layer has already commoditised to $0.06-$0.15 per lot (Gavelist, AuctionWriter, Estimint, all fetched today), which means the description is now free and the only thing left worth charging for is the number.
buyer: Regional and online-only auction houses, estate liquidators, house-clearance firms, probate and insurance valuers, pawnbrokers and volume resellers — anyone who must put a defensible number on second-hand goods at volume. Reachability is proven by the incumbents' own funnels: AuctionWriter starts free at 50 lots/month with self-serve signup and mobile apps; Estimint offers a free plan of 200 listings, 'set up in minutes, no credit card required'; Gavelist sells pay-as-you-go at $0.15/lot (all fetched today). These are self-serve businesses selling to the same buyer, which removes the question of whether this buyer will swipe a card without a call. Batch volume is inherent: AuctionWriter's tiers run to 31,000 new lots per month per customer.
market_evidence: Money changes hands for the lot-level document today, at published, self-serve, per-lot prices: Gavelist $0.15/lot pay-as-you-go and ~$0.08/lot at scale ($79/mo for ~1,000 lots); AuctionWriter free for 50 lots then $99/mo for 1,000 (~$0.10/lot) escalating to $1,689/mo for 31,000; Estimint free 200 listings, $29/mo for 300, $89/mo for 1,500 (~$0.06/lot), $149/mo for 3,500, $249/mo for 5,000 (all fetched today). Separately, money changes hands for the *number* on its own: Swift Values sells single-item valuations from £25+VAT and Mearto sells per-item expert appraisals (both fetched today). The two prices are two orders of magnitude apart — 6-15 cents for the prose, £25 for the judgement — which is exactly where a machine-produced, evidence-cited, error-rated judgement should sit.
incumbents: (1) Gavelist — $0.15/lot pay-as-you-go, ~$0.08/lot at scale, $79/mo for ~1,000 lots, takes 0% of hammer (fetched 2026-08-20). Gap: sells titles/descriptions; its own guide concedes estimate 'quality varies widely' and tells buyers to self-test. (2) AuctionWriter — free 50 lots; $99/mo 1,000 lots; $189/2,200; $289/3,500; up to $1,689/mo for 31,000; exports to 18+ platforms; self-serve with iOS/Android apps (fetched 2026-08-20). Gap: generates 'estimated value' with no stated methodology and no accuracy claim. (3) Estimint — free 200 listings; $29/300; $89/1,500; $149/3,500; $249/5,000; +$19/seat; exports to AuctionFlex, Proxibid, LiveAuctioneers; advertises 'market-based low-high ranges' and research links to eBay sold / Invaluable comps (fetched 2026-08-20). Gap: research links are shown to a human to check; no retrieval-grounded number, no published accuracy. (4) Appraizely — AI estimates over 5M+ auction records, 870+ categories, subscription (fetched 2026-08-20; /pricing 404 today). Gap: single-item collector research surface, not a batch pipeline with CSV export into auction platforms, and no error rate. (5) Circuit Auction AI and Bidsquare Cloud — 'contact sales' and unpublished respectively (search results + Gavelist guide, 2026-08-20). Gap: both fail self-serve outright. (6) Mearto — human specialists, per item (fetched 2026-08-20). Gap: human, therefore not batch. The named flank: five tools compete on writing the description and none publishes a single number about how right its estimates are.
moat: The fine-tune plus the eval harness, and the reason the fine-tune wins is structural rather than rhetorical. A frontier generalist asked 'what will this fetch' answers from a diffuse prior with no retrieval basis, no locality (the same sideboard clears different money in Chelsea and in Carlisle), and no way to be certified. Our model retrieves against an index of what comparable lots actually realised, then a calibration head converts retrieval density into an interval with honest width. The eval harness is the product's public face: a live scoreboard of range-hit rate, median absolute percentage error and coverage, computed on rolling held-out recent sales and broken down by category, so a buyer can see where we are good (mid-century furniture, mass-market ceramics) and where we are not (studio pottery, tribal art) before spending anything. Second, the compounding layer no prose-generator can copy: customers' own realised prices flow back after each sale, giving us a prediction→outcome loop on lots we have already seen, region-tagged and house-tagged. Third, workflow depth: multi-image joint reasoning per lot (the API accepts up to 600 images per request), damage and restoration detection, and structured export into the platforms the incumbents already list.
inference_economics: ~3 photos per lot at 1296 visual tokens each ≈ 3,900 visual tokens ≈ $0.012 per lot on Sonnet 5 ($3/MTok input), or ~$0.004 on Haiku 4.5 if the lot is simple; Opus 5 is called on maybe 3-5% of lots. Stage 2 costs no API money at all — retrieval and calibration run on our own weights on our own GPU, so the marginal cost of the valuation itself is amortised infrastructure, not per-call spend. All-in ≈ $0.02-0.03 per lot against a $0.30 price: ~90% margin, and the margin is structurally better than the incumbents' because the expensive part of our answer is a local index lookup rather than a long generative call. The encoder is small enough that a WebGPU client-side variant is a credible later move for customers who will not send photos to a third party.
autonomy_case: A1: self-serve signup, free 100-lot back-test on the customer's own sold history, card checkout, API key issued by code. A2: batch in, CSV out, no human in the loop. A3: coverage is the degradation mechanism and it is honest by construction — every lot returns a coverage score and the comparables behind it; below 3 comparables the lot is returned as 'no market basis' with the description only, is excluded from the priced set, and is not billed; interval width scales with retrieval dispersion so an uncertain lot returns a visibly wide range rather than a confident wrong one; category-level accuracy is published so a buyer knows in advance which of their lots we should not be trusted on. A4: the comparables index re-ingests daily, the calibration head re-fits weekly, and the eval scoreboard recomputes automatically on rolling held-out sales — nobody maintains a rules file. A5/A6: unattended; zero human minutes per customer.
pricing_hypothesis: $0.30 per valued lot pay-as-you-go, $0.25 at 5,000+/month, billed only on lots that clear the coverage threshold. Deliberately priced 2-4x above the $0.06-$0.15 cataloguing tools because it is a different product — they sell prose, we sell an error-rated number — and deliberately far below the £25+VAT a human charges per item. First 100 lots free as the back-test. Optional $99/mo flat for firms wanting predictable billing under ~400 lots.
distribution: Zero-human channels only. name: Classfile
one_liner: Upload your catalog spreadsheet and your datasheet PDFs; get back an ETIM-classified, validator-clean BMEcat/xChange file your wholesaler's data pool accepts — with every generated value citing the page it came from.
product_form: Standalone web app + REST API (no PIM to migrate into, no browser extension). UX: drop an Excel/CSV of SKUs plus a folder of datasheet PDFs (or product-page URLs), pick the ETIM release and a recipient profile (generic ETIM BMEcat 4.0, ETIM xChange, 2BA/NL, ITEK/DE). A job page then shows, per SKU, the assigned ETIM class, each filled feature with a source-page thumbnail and a confidence score, and a live validation report; the download button unlocks only when the file passes validation, and anything under threshold is left blank on a short 'needs one decision' list instead of being invented.
ai_core: Frontier API, cheap tier, three stages. (1) Classification: multilingual embeddings over the free ETIM model's class descriptions + synonyms shortlist ~25 candidate classes, then a Haiku-4.5 / Gemini-Flash-Lite-class call picks one with structured output and an explicit abstain option. (2) Feature filling: for the chosen class we load its exact feature schema (feature codes, types — logical/numeric/range/alphanumeric — allowed value lists and units, all from the ODC-BY-licensed ETIM release) and the SKU's evidence (datasheet pages as images/PDF, product page text, existing spec columns); the model emits only values drawn from the class's allowed list, each with a provenance pointer (file, page, snippet) and confidence. (3) Deterministic assembly + validation in code: ETIM BMEcat 4.0 XML / ETIM xChange JSON built by a template, then checked against the XSD plus model constraints (feature belongs to class, value in allowed value list, unit permitted, recipient's mandatory-field profile). Fine-tuned path (phase 2, the real asset): manufacturers already publish ETIM-classified BMEcat/xChange files and wholesaler catalogues expose ETIM class + feature values, so a corpus of (datasheet/description → class code + feature values) pairs can be assembled with the vendors' own codes as labels — zero human labelling. Target ~200k–1M labelled article records; LoRA a small open model for stage 1 and the high-frequency classes of stage 2, keeping the frontier model for the long tail. Eval harness is per-class accuracy on held-out real classified articles.
why_now: Two capabilities, both dated. (a) Vision-language document parsing plus long context at commodity price: Claude Haiku 4.5 is $1/$5 per MTok ($0.50/$2.50 on the Batch API) and takes PDFs natively; Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite is $0.10/$0.40 per MTok ($0.05/$0.20 batched) — both verified on the vendors' own pricing pages on 2026-08-20. Holding a 30-feature class schema plus a datasheet in context and emitting schema-constrained JSON costs fractions of a cent; pre-2023 this had to be hand-coded rules per class across 5,500+ ETIM classes, which is why the work is still done by hand or offshored. (b) The reference model became free and machine-readable: the ETIM Classification Model is published under the Open Data Commons Attribution Licence, downloadable without login (ETIM 10.0 releases dated 2024-12-05 and 2025-08-05) and served by a live REST API (etimapi.etim-international.com v2, swagger fetched today).
buyer: Manufacturers and importers of electrotechnical, HVAC/plumbing, building-materials, tools and shipbuilding products with roughly 500–50,000 SKUs that sell through wholesalers. ETIM International lists twenty member organisations covering twenty-one countries and a model in seventeen languages (about-us page, fetched 2026-08-20), and ETIM North America states that Sonepar, Rexel and WESCO 'increasingly expect ETIM-classified data from their suppliers'. Reachability is proven by how these buyers already transact: 2BA publishes 2026 manufacturer contract rates online, and ETIM-Mapper sells through a public price calculator — no procurement committee, a product-data manager with a card and a wholesaler deadline.
market_evidence: Money is already moving for the distribution of this exact data, before anyone generates it: 2BA (the Dutch ETIM data pool) charges manufacturers €2,150–€2,529/yr for the Logo-Deeplink contract and €2,756–€5,070/yr for the 2BA & ETIM Combi contract, plus a €250 one-off, at 2026 rates (fetched 2026-08-20). Tooling to author the data is bought self-serve today: ETIM-Mapper's live price API returns €1,228/yr for 1,000 products on its cheapest tier, €1,890/yr standard, and €6,652/yr at 20,000 products (queried directly 2026-08-20). nextPIM sells manufacturer plans at €600/€1,200/€1,800 per month (1,000 products on the entry plan). Rastro AI charges 'starting at $1,000/month' for up to 1,000 SKUs. So a 5,000-SKU manufacturer is already spending €3k–€25k/yr on data pool fees plus authoring tools, and the classification labour on top.
incumbents: Five closest, all fetched 2026-08-20. (1) Rastro AI — AI catalog-ops platform that reads datasheets and maps to ETIM; pricing page says manufacturers 'starting at $1,000/month' (site copy also quotes $500/mo ≤1k SKUs, $2,000/mo ≤10k), distributors $1,000/mo platform fee + $1.50→$0.65 per SKU; demo-only, 'dedicated implementation team', white-glove first month. Gap: humans in the loop by design — fails our A6 shape, and prices out a 2,000-SKU supplier. (2) nextPIM (DE) — €600/€1,200/€1,800 per month with 'KI-Funktionen'; every plan button is 'Jetzt anfragen' (request a quote), and it is a full PIM you must move into. Gap: no self-serve purchase, no output guarantee. (3) ETIM-Mapper — purpose-built ETIM/xChange/BMEcat tool with import/export/validation and an ETIM v10 migration assistant, €1,228–€8,647/yr by tier and product count. Gap: it is an editor — a human still picks the class and types the feature values; nothing is generated from a datasheet. (4) Sales Layer — markets an 'AI Suite' with Categorization, Data Quality and Translations; plan table shows Scale/Premium/Enterprise SKU caps but no price, 'Get a quote', no online payment. Gap: sales-led, and categorization is generic, not ETIM-release-bound. (5) Plytix — self-serve PIM, Free 500 SKUs / Pro $499/mo 50,000 SKUs, AI credits at '$10 per 1,000', Product Data Sheets add-on $200/mo. Gap: AI credits are copy/image edits; no ETIM class model, no BMEcat output, no validator. Adjacent AI-native entrant to watch: Anglera (fills a category's attribute schema SKU-by-SKU with provenance, '~30 days' implementation, pushes into your existing PIM) — same technique, enterprise motion. None of the five sells a file with a pass/fail validation guarantee.
moat: Not the prompt. Three compounding assets. (a) The assembled corpus: publicly published ETIM BMEcat/xChange files and wholesaler catalogue data give (document → class + feature values) pairs already labelled by the vendors themselves; that corpus fine-tunes a small open classifier for the ~500 highest-volume classes and, more importantly, becomes the per-class eval harness — precision on class assignment, per-feature fill accuracy, unit correctness, hallucinated-value rate, all measured against real classified articles. A generalist chat model cannot certify any of that, and neither can an editor like ETIM-Mapper. (b) The recipient profile library: which fields 2BA, ITEK, or a given wholesaler treats as mandatory, and the release-to-release deltas (ETIM 9→10 migration is a forced re-classification event with a datable trigger). (c) Usage data: every correction a customer makes on the 'needs one decision' list is a labelled hard example, so the abstain threshold falls over time and margin rises. The commercial expression of the moat is the guarantee: we only ship files that pass validation, and we refund the credits for any delivered file a recipient's validator rejects — a promise only someone running the eval harness can make.
inference_economics: Per SKU: ~8k input tokens (class schema 2–4k + datasheet evidence 3–5k, with the class schema prompt-cached across all SKUs in the same class) and ~500 output tokens. Claude Haiku 4.5 on the Batch API ($0.50/$2.50 per MTok, fetched 2026-08-20) = ~$0.0053/SKU; Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite batched ($0.05/$0.20, fetched 2026-08-20) = ~$0.0005/SKU. A 10,000-SKU catalogue therefore costs $5–$53 of inference against a €399 price point — >90% gross margin even before caching, and the phase-2 fine-tuned classifier moves stage 1 onto our own small model at near-zero marginal cost. Local WebGPU is not the wedge here (this is a server-side batch job on files the customer uploads), but a self-hosted small model is the cost floor if API prices move.
autonomy_case: A1: Stripe checkout, no demo — the free tier (validate any BMEcat/xChange file, classify 25 SKUs) is the whole sales process. A2: fulfilment is a queue worker — parse, embed, classify, extract, assemble, validate, deliver. A3 degradation is the core design, not an afterthought: every generated value carries a provenance pointer and confidence; below threshold the field is emitted empty and listed for the customer, never guessed; the class assignment shows the runner-up classes; and no file is downloadable until the deterministic validator passes, with the report shown in full. Failure mode is 'fewer fields filled', never 'a wrong spec in a wholesaler's catalogue'. Credits are auto-refunded if a delivered file is rejected by a recipient's validator. A4: nightly ingest of the free ETIM model releases and the ETIM API keeps classes, features, values and units current, including new releases. A5: unattended workers, retries, dead-letter queue. A6: no onboarding call — recipient profiles are config we maintain once for everyone.
pricing_hypothesis: Credit-based, self-serve. Free: unlimited file validation + 25 SKUs classified. Starter €99/mo — 1,000 SKU-enrichments. Growth €399/mo — 10,000. Scale €999/mo — 50,000. Overage €0.02/SKU. One-off 'ETIM 9→10 migration' packs at €0.03/SKU. This lands at roughly one-tenth of Rastro's $1,000/mo-for-1,000-SKUs and below nextPIM's €600/mo entry, while doing the part those tools leave to a human.
distribution: Zero-human channels only. (1) SEO/AEO against a set of queries with clear commercial intent and no good free answer: 'ETIM classification', 'BMEcat 4.0 example file', 'ETIM 9 to 10 migration', 'wholesaler rejected my product data'. (2) Free tools as the funnel and as link bait: a BMEcat/xChange validator, an ETIM class/feature browser, and an ETIM 9→10 diff — each of which is also the eval harness's public face. (3) Listings in software-supplier registries of the data pools and national ETIM organisations, plus Product Hunt and the PIM/product-data communities. AP1: a generalist assistant cannot classify 10,000 SKUs to a 5,500-class taxonomy, hold each class's allowed-value list, emit a schema-valid XML file, and prove per-class accuracy — this is batch scale + structured output flowing into someone else's ingestion system + a vertical eval a chat product cannot certify. AP2: there is no page to summarise; the artefact is a file destined for a data pool, and an agentic browser has nothing to act on.
risks: AP6: the ETIM model is ODC-BY (free, attribution required), but the official xChange validation and BMEcat certification tools are member-gated — we must implement our own validator from the published XSD and model (fine, and it is the moat) and join a national ETIM organisation to hand customers an official certificate; some national language versions may require national membership. Model deprecation and API price moves are absorbed by the eval harness (swap models, re-run the per-class suite) and by the fine-tuned fallback. Competitive: Rastro and Anglera are AI-native and could drop to self-serve pricing; the data pools themselves are moving in — ITEK markets 'KI-basierte ETIM Services' and nextPIM already ships 'KI-Funktionen'. Legal: assembling the training corpus from published catalogues needs a clean source policy (manufacturers' own published BMEcat downloads first, wholesaler pages only where terms allow). Buyer conservatism is real — EU product-data managers may want a person to blame, which is precisely why the refund-on-rejection guarantee has to be in the checkout flow. NOT yet proven: that these buyers will pay without a call; the true per-class accuracy ceiling on messy scanned datasheets; and whether the recipient-specific mandatory-field profiles can be maintained from public documentation alone.

name: Feedwright
one_liner: Hand over your timetable PDFs and your stop list; get back a GTFS feed that scores zero errors on the canonical validator, hosted at a stable URL and regenerated at every service change.
product_form: Standalone web app. UX: upload timetable PDFs/spreadsheets and a stop list (addresses or a map pin session), and the job returns a full GTFS zip plus a review canvas where every parsed trip is shown beside the timetable cell it came from and every matched stop beside its OpenStreetMap candidate. Publishing gives a permanent feed URL that trip planners poll; a re-run at the next service change diffs against the previous feed so the operator can see exactly what changed.
ai_core: Frontier API vision model for the hard half — parsing timetable grids (multi-column, footnoted, holiday-variant, frequency-based) into (route, service pattern, stop sequence, times) — plus a ranking call for stop-name → coordinate matching against OpenStreetMap candidates. Everything after that is deterministic code: calendar/calendar_dates expansion, trip and stop_times assembly, shapes from routed geometry, then the Canonical GTFS Schedule Validator run in-loop, with its error codes fed back as repair instructions until the feed is clean. Fine-tuned path: the Mobility Database catalogues 6,000+ open GTFS feeds across 99 countries, and the agencies behind them also publish the human timetables those feeds encode — pairing them yields a supervised corpus (timetable page → stop_times rows, stop name → coordinates) with no human labelling, enough to LoRA a small open model for the parsing and matching stages and, more importantly, to build the eval harness: round-trip accuracy (regenerate the printed timetable from the produced feed and diff it against the source page).
why_now: Timetable grids are the classic OCR failure case — merged headers, footnote markers, columns that mean 'this trip does not serve this stop', holiday footers — and reliable extraction only became possible with vision-language document parsing; TransitGPT (Springer, Public Transport, 2025) applies LLMs to querying GTFS, and nothing yet goes the other direction from documents to a feed. The economics arrived with it: a 100-page timetable set is ~250k input tokens, which is $0.13 at Claude Haiku 4.5 batch rates and $0.0125 at Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite batch rates (both fetched 2026-08-20). The acceptance test also matured: MobilityData's Canonical GTFS Schedule Validator is free, open-source and versioned on GitHub, so 'correct' is a machine verdict, not an opinion.
buyer: Small transit agencies and private operators that need to appear in Google Maps, Apple Maps, Transit and Moovit: rural/tribal and small-city agencies, university and hospital shuttles, airport and hotel shuttles, intercity coach carriers, ferries and seasonal tourist services. Sizing signals: the Mobility Database catalogues 6,000+ GTFS/GTFS-RT/GBFS feeds across 99 countries (i.e. the installed base of publishers), National RTAP builds a free tool specifically because rural and tribal agencies lack the resources, and GTFS·X's own homepage claims '~45% of U.S. transit agencies don't' have a feed (competitor marketing — treat as a directional claim, not a verified number). Self-serve reachable by card for private operators; public agencies can pay by card at these ticket sizes but some will insist on a PO, which is the main A1 friction.
market_evidence: TransitWiki (the industry's own reference) states: 'The cost for a transit agency to hire a vendor or consultant to create GTFS data is usually around $200-$500 per route.' National RTAP's free GTFS Builder quantifies the labour it replaces — 'approximately 4 hours per route initially, with 4 hours annually for maintenance' of manual Excel entry across 12 data tabs. And self-serve software at this altitude already sells: GTFS·X lists a free browser editor and a Planner plan at $299/mo ($2,988/yr) with a 14-day trial, while its own comparison table shows Trillium and the enterprise platforms as 'Quote' only.
incumbents: Five closest, fetched 2026-08-20. (1) National RTAP GTFS Builder — free Excel-based builder plus free phone/email expert support for rural and tribal agencies; ~4 hours per route of manual entry, requires Google Earth Pro familiarity. Gap: it is the manual labour we automate; free but expensive in hours. (2) GTFS·X — Editor $0, Planner $299/mo / $2,988/yr, self-serve with live spec validation and GTFS-Flex authoring. Gap: a map-based editor and service planner — you still author the schedule by hand; nothing ingests an existing PDF timetable. (3) Trillium Solutions — tools plus full-service feed creation and GTFS-RT; no public price (fetched page lists services only), i.e. a consulting motion. Gap: humans per customer, quote-gated. (4) TransLoc Architect — free web-based GTFS creation tool per TransitWiki's tool list. Gap: manual authoring, vendor-adjacent. (5) Optibus / Remix (Via) — enterprise scheduling platforms, listed as 'Quote' in GTFS·X's competitor table and sold via demo. Gap: priced and sold for agencies far above this segment. No incumbent in this list converts documents to a validator-clean feed automatically — the AI-native slot is empty (searches for an LLM PDF-timetable-to-GTFS tool returned only the reverse direction, GTFS→timetable, and TransitGPT for querying).
moat: The eval harness is unusually literal here: the Canonical GTFS Schedule Validator is the acceptance test, and we run it inside the loop, so the product's claim ('zero errors, or you don't pay') is machine-checkable by the customer too. Underneath: the assembled corpus from the 6,000+ open feeds paired with the operators' published timetables gives (a) fine-tuning data for the grid parser and the stop matcher, and (b) a regression suite of real feeds — regenerate a known feed from its own published timetable and diff. Usage compounds: every stop a customer re-pins is a labelled hard example for the matcher, and every service-change re-run is a fresh document/feed pair. Workflow depth adds the rest — hosted stable feed URLs, change diffs, and Mobility Database registration are things a chat model cannot hold.
inference_economics: A 100-page timetable set is ~250k input tokens of images plus ~40k output tokens of structured rows: $0.23 at Claude Haiku 4.5 batch rates ($0.50/$2.50 per MTok) or ~$0.02 at Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite batch rates ($0.05/$0.20), both fetched 2026-08-20; stop-matching adds a few thousand short calls. Even with three repair passes and a stronger model for hard pages, a converted feed costs well under $2 against a $149-per-route conversion price. Marginal cost of the monthly hosting tier is storage and a validator run — effectively zero.
autonomy_case: A1: card checkout, free tier is 'validate and host your existing feed'. A2: fulfilment is a pipeline job. A3: the product degrades in-product by construction — trips whose times cannot be read confidently are flagged rather than guessed, unmatched stops are shown as ranked OSM candidates on a map with the source line beside them, and no feed is publishable until the canonical validator reports zero ERRORs (WARNINGs and INFOs are surfaced with explanations); refund if a delivered feed fails the validator. A4: the validator rules and GTFS spec are pulled from their public GitHub releases; stop geometry from OpenStreetMap, both self-refreshing. A5/A6: unattended workers; no onboarding call — the review canvas is the onboarding.
pricing_hypothesis: $149 per route converted (one-off), plus $39/month per operator for hosting, monthly revalidation, service-change re-runs and feed diffs. Free: validate and host an existing feed. That undercuts the $200–$500/route consultant rate cited by TransitWiki while replacing the ~4 hours/route of manual entry National RTAP documents, and sits below GTFS·X's $299/mo for operators who want a feed rather than a planning suite.
distribution: Zero-human channels: SEO against 'how to create a GTFS feed', 'GTFS validator errors explained', 'get my shuttle into Google Maps' — each landing on the free validator/host tool; listing the produced feeds in the Mobility Database (the catalogue trip planners read, which makes every delivered feed a referral surface); tool listings on community resource pages (gtfs.org resources, TransitWiki's tool list) that already enumerate free and paid tools; and transit/mobility forums and university-shuttle communities. AP1: a chat assistant cannot emit an eight-file, tens-of-thousands-of-rows feed that passes an external validator, nor geocode a hundred stop names against OSM — batch scale and structured output into someone else's ingestion pipeline. AP2: nothing here is 'summarise this page'; the artefact is a published data feed.
risks: Weakest of the two on commercial gravity, and I flag it honestly. Free substitutes are real and funded: National RTAP's GTFS Builder is free with free human support, GTFS·X gives away a full browser editor, and both could add document ingestion (GTFS·X moves fast and already ships live spec validation). Buyer friction: public agencies often buy by PO and grant cycle, which strains A1; purchase frequency is low (a conversion plus service-change re-runs, not daily usage), so the hosting tier has to carry retention. TAM is modest — thousands of operators, not hundreds of thousands. Quality risk concentrates in geometry (shapes, stop placement) rather than text, and a wrong stop coordinate is visible to riders, so the abstain thresholds must be conservative. AP6: GTFS is a stable community spec (low deprecation risk), but Google's Transit partner onboarding terms and the validator's rule changes are outside our control. NOT proven: that private operators, rather than agencies, are the paying segment; and the achievable first-pass validator-clean rate on genuinely messy scanned timetables.

name: PanelFill
one_liner: A browser extension that turns a clinician's document dossier into a provenance-tagged 200-field provider record and fills CAQH/DataSpring, PECOS/CMS-855, Medicaid and commercial payer enrollment forms field-by-field — inside the credentialing coordinator's own authenticated session, never clicking submit.
product_form: Chrome/Edge MV3 extension + a thin web app that holds the dossier vault and audit log. UX: drop a provider's PDFs (state licenses, DEA, board certs, CV, malpractice COI, W-9, diploma, ECFMG, voided check) into the vault once; the model builds a normalized provider record where every field carries a source (document, page, snippet) and a confidence. Then on any enrollment form — CAQH Provider Data Portal, PECOS, a state Medicaid portal, a payer's web application, or a CMS-855 PDF — you press Fill: the extension maps live form fields to dossier elements, fills what it is sure of, leaves the rest blank with the exact question and candidate answers surfaced in a side panel, and stamps a provenance chip on each filled field. It never presses Submit or Attest.
ai_core: Two model tiers. (1) Dossier ingestion: Claude Sonnet 5 vision on the raw PDFs/scans, emitting a structured provider record with per-field citations and confidence (~$2/MTok in, $10/MTok out, fetched from platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing on 2026-08-20). (2) Fill-time field mapping: a fine-tuned small model that takes {form field label, sibling DOM/label context, section heading, form fingerprint} and emits {canonical provider-data element, transform, confidence}. Base: a 4–8B open instruct model served cheaply, or WebGPU-local once distilled. Dataset we can assemble autonomously: (a) every public CMS enrollment form (855A/855B/855I/855R) and all 50 state Medicaid provider-enrollment PDFs — public, downloadable, re-crawlable; (b) the CAQH/DataSpring data-element set; (c) DOM field-label captures from live use, auto-labeled by the frontier model at fill time and then CORRECTED BY THE USER'S OWN EDITS — every correction is a free gold label. Target 150k–400k (field-context → element) pairs within 12 months; bootstrap at launch with ~40k synthetic pairs generated by the frontier model from the public form corpus. Eval harness: held-out forms scored on per-field exact match and, more importantly, WRONG-FILL RATE (a wrong value is far worse than a blank), which is the metric the fine-tune is optimized against and the confidence threshold is calibrated to.
why_now: Three capabilities that did not exist before ~2023 and only matured this year: (1) vision-language parsing of heterogeneous scanned credentials — a photographed nursing license, a malpractice COI, an ECFMG certificate — into structured fields with citations; (2) reliable structured output + tool use so the mapping flows into a form-filling API instead of prose; (3) first-party browser/computer-use tooling: Anthropic's `browser_toolset_20260801` and `computer_toolset_20260801` are dated 2026-08-01 in the pricing docs fetched today, i.e. agentic browser control became a supported, priced primitive this month. Separately, a Chromium fix merged in June 2026 for Chrome's own Gemini agent failing to fill form fields (chromestory.com, fetched 2026-08-20) shows the general-agent form-fill path is still being debugged in production — the vertical, provenance-bearing version is the opening.
buyer: Not the solo therapist (Headway/Alma-style networks absorb that credentialing for free, and MedSole RCM will do it done-for-you at $99/payer — fetched 2026-08-20). The buyer is the team that fills these forms hundreds of times a month: (a) credentialing/enrollment departments inside medical billing and claims-processing firms — IBISWorld's Medical Claims Processing Services page, fetched directly 2026-08-20 (HTTP 200), carries 3,735 US businesses for 2026; (b) in-house credentialing coordinators at 10–300 provider groups, behavioral-health groups and telehealth companies. Self-serve reachable: these are Stripe-card buyers who already install browser extensions, and they congregate in public forums (r/CodingandBilling, credentialing Facebook groups) rather than behind procurement.
market_evidence: Money is already changing hands for exactly this labor, at a published unit price. MedSole RCM publishes 'provider enrollment and credentialing services start at $99 per payer', covering CAQH ProView setup, NPPES taxonomy verification, PECOS enrollment, commercial payer applications and behavioral-health carve-outs across '900+ payer networks' (medsolercm.com, fetched 2026-08-20). Broader published ranges from credentialing service vendors: $100–$300 per provider per payer, $1,500–$3,000 flat for a 5-payer behavioral-health panel, $600–$2,400/yr ongoing maintenance per provider. The work is also structurally recurring, not one-shot: CAQH/DataSpring requires re-attestation every 120 days regardless of whether anything changed, and a lapse flags the profile to every payer pulling data — so each provider generates repeat form work forever, not one application.
incumbents: Five closest, all checked live on 2026-08-20: (1) Medallion — pricing page fetched, no published price, 'custom engagement model', demo/sales required; raised $43M to build a national credentialing clearinghouse (prnewswire). (2) Verifiable — verifiable.com fetched, no pricing published anywhere, 'Book a Demo' motion, positioned for health plans and orgs at '100 providers, or 1 million'. (3) Assured (withassured.com) — fetched, no pricing page at all, demo-gated, targets digital health / health systems / health plans. (4) MedTrainer — pricing page fetched, three tiers named but zero USD figures, 'Request a Quote', 24–48h quote turnaround, phone number as the CTA. (5) Kaizen Automation — the closest functional competitor: it explicitly automates 'CAQH re-attestation, payer application submissions, status checks' as browser portal automation, but runs plain-English workflows on CLOUD browsers, prices 'Custom (ROI-based)', and gates entry behind a Calendly 'Book a call' (fetched 2026-08-20). Gap left: every one of the five is demo-gated with no published price, and the only portal-automation player runs headless cloud browsers rather than acting inside the coordinator's own sanctioned Practice Administrator session. Chrome Web Store: a store and Google search on 2026-08-20 surfaced no credentialing- or payer-enrollment-specific autofill extension — only generic autofill tools (AutoFill Forms, Autofill.Ai, AI Form Filler, docFiller) and unrelated 'credential management' extensions. There is no self-serve, per-application-priced product in this category today.
moat: Three layers, none of which is a prompt. (1) The assembled corpus: every public CMS-855 form and all 50 state Medicaid enrollment forms, plus accumulated DOM fingerprints of the payer portals our users actually touch — a form-map library that compounds with every customer and that no generalist can enumerate. (2) The fine-tune: a small field-mapping model trained on (field-context → canonical element) pairs, where the training signal is the user's own corrections at fill time. It beats a frontier generalist on this task in the ways that matter operationally — it is ~50x cheaper per field so it can run on every field of a 10-page application, it is deterministic across re-fills of the same form, and it is calibrated: the eval harness measures wrong-fill rate on held-out forms, which lets us set per-field abstention thresholds. A generalist chat model can neither certify nor abstain against that metric because it has never seen the form corpus. (3) Usage-accumulated provider records: once a credentialing shop's 400 providers are in the vault with provenance, switching cost is the vault, not the extension.
inference_economics: Priced against Claude rates fetched 2026-08-20 (Sonnet 5 $2/$10 per MTok; Haiku 4.5 $1/$5; cache reads at 0.1x input; Batch API 50% off). Dossier ingestion, once per provider: ~25 scanned pages ≈ 37.5k vision input + ~4k structured output on Sonnet 5 ≈ $0.12. Per form page at fill time: ~12k tokens of field context + a cached dossier record (cache read ≈ $0.001) + ~2.5k output ≈ $0.05 on Sonnet 5, ≈ $0.025 on Haiku 4.5. A full 8-page payer application ≈ $0.30–$0.50 all-in; a CAQH re-attestation diff ≈ $0.05. Against a $99 human per-payer service and a $199/mo product tier covering 150 applications, COGS is ~$60/mo worst case — and once the fine-tuned mapper carries the routine fields (frontier reserved for the initial dossier read and low-confidence fields), marginal cost falls roughly 5–10x. A WebGPU-local variant of the mapper is a credible later step: it makes the field-mapping stage zero-marginal-cost and lets us tell a PHI-minimizing story, though the initial vision pass stays server-side.
autonomy_case: A1: Stripe checkout, click-through BAA, extension install, done — no call. A2: fulfilment is the extension plus the API; nothing is hand-produced. A3 degradation is the core design, because a wrong credentialing field is worse than a blank one: every field carries confidence and a source chip; below threshold the field is LEFT BLANK and the side panel shows the raw question, the candidate values, and the document snippet each came from; the tool never presses Attest or Submit — the human licensed to attest does; wrong-fill rate is the tracked eval metric and is displayed to the customer; if an application is rejected for a data error on a field we filled above threshold, the account is auto-credited by code. A4: reference data self-maintains — NPPES publishes monthly and weekly full-file and deactivation downloads free and without login (download.cms.gov/nppes/NPI_Files.html fetched 2026-08-20, HTTP 200, last-modified 2026-08-17, current dissemination file dated 2026-08-10), so NPI/taxonomy/address checks refresh on a cron; CMS-855 and state Medicaid form PDFs are re-crawled and diffed; portal DOM fingerprints self-invalidate on change and re-derive via the frontier model. A5: unattended — crawl, diff, re-label, re-eval on schedule. A6: zero human minutes per customer.
pricing_hypothesis: Self-serve, usage-shaped: Free — 1 provider, 3 filled applications/month (this is also the acquisition wedge). Solo $49/mo — 25 applications. Team $199/mo — 5 seats, 150 applications. Shop $599/mo — unlimited seats, 600 applications, audit-log export. Overage $0.75/application. Anchored explicitly against the $99/payer done-for-you price: a shop paying a VA an hour per application replaces ~$60 of labor with ~$1 of software.
distribution: Zero-human channels. (1) Chrome Web Store listing targeting the exact uncontested queries — 'CAQH autofill', 'payer enrollment', 'CMS-855', 'credentialing autofill' — where the store currently returns only generic autofill tools. (2) Free-tier wedges that are useful alone and generate the dossier: a free CAQH/DataSpring re-attestation tracker (the 120-day clock is a recurring, dateable hook), and a free 'provider data mismatch checker' built on the monthly NPPES file that flags where a group's roster disagrees with NPPES — pure SEO bait that self-maintains. (3) SEO on long-tail form questions ('how to fill CMS-855I section 4B', state Medicaid enrollment walkthroughs), each page shipping the filler. (4) Communities: r/CodingandBilling, r/MedicalCoding, credentialing Facebook groups, NAMSS-adjacent forums. AP1: this is not one question for one user — it is 150–600 applications a month per account, each producing a structured record and an audit trail that flows into the customer's credentialing tracker; a $20/mo chat subscription cannot be embedded at the point of fill, cannot abstain on calibrated confidence, and cannot certify a wrong-fill rate. AP2: the answers are not on the page. They are in a 200-field dossier assembled from scanned credentials, and the required output is a provenance-stamped fill an attesting human can audit — that is the opposite of 'summarize/act on this page'. Chrome's Gemini fills forms from data the USER explicitly shared with Google; it does not read a malpractice COI PDF, map it to CAQH element semantics, cite the page it came from, or abstain.
risks: AP6 platform risk: (a) Chrome Web Store limited-use policy (fetched 2026-08-20) restricts collection of browsing activity to prominently disclosed user-facing features and forbids transferring user data to third parties outside delivering the disclosed function — our single purpose must be narrowly declared and the dossier must never be repurposed; direct human review of user data is also prohibited, which happens to align with A6. (b) Portal terms: the CAQH Provider Data Portal terms (dataspring.com, fetched 2026-08-20) contain no explicit anti-automation clause we could find and explicitly sanction Practice Administrators inputting information on a provider's behalf — our shape (acting inside the administrator's own authenticated session, never holding credentials) sits in the sanctioned lane, but individual payer portals may prohibit automated entry and this must be checked per portal before shipping a fill target. (c) CAQH rebranded to DataSpring; portal DOMs and CMS forms change without notice — mitigated by fingerprint invalidation, but it is real maintenance. (d) Model deprecation/price shift: mitigated by the fine-tuned mapper carrying the bulk of volume. NOT YET PROVEN: the buyer count. 3,735 claims-processing businesses is a floor, not a validated ICP size, and I could not source a count of in-house credentialing teams at 10–300 provider groups — the first thing to test is whether 50 such shops will pay $199–599/mo. Also unproven: whether shops paying $99/payer will buy tooling rather than simply keep the VA, and whether the wrong-fill rate can be driven low enough that a coordinator trusts the fill instead of re-checking every field (if they re-check everything, the time saving collapses). PHI/BAA: enrollment dossiers are mostly provider data, not patient data, which keeps HIPAA exposure lower than a clinical product — but Anthropic's BAA covers the API only in HIPAA-ready configuration, so the compliance posture must be built in from day one, not retrofitted.

name: BindSheet
one_liner: An extension for small commercial-lines insurance agencies that reads the ACORD PDFs and loss runs for an account once, then fills each carrier's quoting portal from that single extracted submission — in the agent's own logged-in carrier session, with every field traceable back to the ACORD page it came from.
product_form: Chrome/Edge MV3 extension plus a per-account submission workspace. UX: drop the ACORD 125/126/130/140, the loss runs and the expiring dec page onto an account; the model extracts one canonical submission record with page-level citations. Then open Travelers', Hartford's or Chubb's agent portal and press Fill — the extension walks the multi-screen wizard, fills what it can ground in the documents, flags what the carrier asks that the ACORDs do not answer, and produces a per-carrier diff of exactly which fields differed between portals.
ai_core: Claude Sonnet 5 vision for ACORD/loss-run extraction into a canonical commercial submission schema with per-field citations (ACORD forms are standardized, so the extraction target is stable and the ground truth is checkable). A fine-tuned small model handles portal field mapping: {carrier portal fingerprint, field label, screen context} → {canonical ACORD element, transform}. Dataset we can assemble: the ACORD form family is a fixed, published schema — we generate tens of thousands of synthetically populated ACORD forms (varying industries, entity types, coverage structures), render them, and train extraction against known ground truth without a single human label; portal-side mapping labels come from live fills corrected by the CSR. Eval harness: exact-match on synthetic ACORDs with known values, plus wrong-fill rate per carrier portal.
why_now: Reliable vision-language extraction from mixed-quality PDFs and photographed loss runs, plus long context that lets one prompt hold a whole submission packet, plus priced agentic browser tooling (browser_toolset_20260801, dated 2026-08-01 in Anthropic's pricing docs fetched today). Before ~2023, portal filling meant brittle per-carrier RPA scripts that broke on every UI change — which is why the incumbents in this space are services-heavy and enterprise-priced.
buyer: Small and mid-size independent P&C agencies doing commercial lines. Sourced: the Big 'I' Agency Universe Study reports 39,000 independent P&C agencies in the US (2024 study, independentagent.com fetched 2026-08-20), with 51.6% under $500k revenue and 27.1% under $150k — i.e. the majority are too small to be sold by Applied Systems' enterprise motion but large enough to feel the pain. Self-serve reachable: agency principals buy tools on a card and CSRs install extensions. Note the scope discipline: commercial lines only — personal lines already has comparative raters that bridge to carriers, so that half of the market is closed.
market_evidence: Documented labor cost and existing spend. A 14-person commercial-lines brokerage was measured at ~65 minutes per new submission on manual entry across an AMS and three carrier portals, cut to 12 minutes of CSR review after automation; CSRs at non-automated agencies average 47 minutes per quote request versus 11 at automated ones (layer3labs.io and ustechautomations.com, fetched 2026-08-20). The same guide prices existing automation engagements at $2,500 for a single ACORD-intake automation up to $30,000 for a full brokerage stack — money already leaving agencies for this exact job, at project prices a self-serve product undercuts by an order of magnitude.
incumbents: Five closest, checked live 2026-08-20: (1) Relay (relayins.com) — the nearest functional match; its own page says it 'extracts data from submissions, populates carrier portals, and compiles returned quotes', names Travelers/Progressive/Hartford/Safeco and EZLynx/Vertafore/HawkSoft — but there is no pricing, access is a waitlist, and the team decides 'when the workflow is a fit for guided access'. No browser extension mentioned. (2) Applied Indio (useindio.com / appliedsystems.com) — commercial submissions platform, Applied Systems does not publish pricing (its /pricing path 404s; third-party listings cite ~$50/user/mo), sales conversation required; and its job is collecting data FROM the insured via smart forms, not filling carrier portals. (3) FurtherAI — enterprise submission-intake AI, pricing not publicly disclosed, priced per workflow/line of business with implementation fees. (4) Quandri (quandri.io) — fetched: renewal intelligence including 'automatic requoting through carrier portals', but personal-lines renewals, no published pricing, 45-minute discovery demo required. (5) Skyvern (skyvern.com) — the only self-serve substitute, and it is generic: $0 free / $29 Hobby / $149 Pro, ~$0.024 per browser action, and it publicly markets insurance carrier portal automation. Gap left: nobody sells a self-serve, ACORD-grounded, provenance-bearing portal filler to a 4-person commercial agency. Skyvern is generic automation with no ACORD schema, no citations, no per-carrier field library; the four insurance-native players are all demo-gated or waitlisted.
moat: The carrier-portal field-map library (which carrier asks which question on which screen, and which ACORD element answers it) is the accumulating asset — it compounds per fill and cannot be scraped from anywhere because the portals are credentialed. On top of it, the ACORD extraction fine-tune: because ACORD is a published standard, we can mint unlimited labeled training data by generating and rendering synthetic completed forms, which gives us an eval harness with true ground truth that a frontier generalist has no equivalent of. The fine-tune wins on cost-per-field (letting us run on all ~200 fields of a submission), on determinism across re-fills, and on calibrated abstention against a measured wrong-fill rate.
inference_economics: At rates fetched 2026-08-20: ACORD packet extraction ≈ 20 pages vision + structured output on Sonnet 5 ≈ $0.08–0.12 per account, done once. Per carrier portal: ~10 screens × ~8k tokens of field context + ~15k output ≈ $0.31 on Sonnet 5, ≈ $0.15 on Haiku 4.5. Three carriers ≈ $0.60–$1.00 per submission all-in. Against 65 minutes of CSR time and a $99/user/mo price covering 60 submissions, COGS ≈ $60/mo worst case before the fine-tuned mapper. Compare Skyvern's generic $0.024/action: a 200-field submission is ~200+ actions ≈ $5, so a vertical fine-tune is also a straightforward cost win over renting generic automation.
autonomy_case: A1: card checkout, install, fill — no demo. A2: extension + API. A3: every field shows the ACORD form and page it came from; unanswerable carrier questions are surfaced as an explicit 'the ACORDs do not answer this' list rather than guessed; the tool does not press Submit/Bind — the licensed agent does; wrong-fill rate is measured per carrier portal and shown; auto-credit by code if a high-confidence field is wrong. pricing_hypothesis: Free — 5 submissions/month (wedge). Producer $99/user/mo — 60 submissions. Agency $299/mo — unlimited seats, 250 submissions. Overage $1.50/submission. Deliberately positioned an order of magnitude under the $2,500–$30,000 automation project prices agencies are quoted today.
distribution: Chrome Web Store listing on 'ACORD', 'carrier portal', 'commercial submission'. Free-tier wedge: a standalone 'ACORD PDF → structured JSON/CSV' web tool with no login, which is genuinely useful alone, ranks for a high-intent query, and seeds the extraction pipeline. SEO on per-carrier submission walkthroughs and per-ACORD-form field guides. Community: r/InsuranceAgent, Insurance Agency Owners Alliance groups, the Catalyit solution directory. AP1: an agency does hundreds of submissions a month and needs structured output flowing into an AMS with an audit trail — not one chat answer. AP2: carrier portals are credentialed agent portals; Google cannot point Gemini at them, and the answers come from ACORD PDFs and loss runs the browser has never seen. The extension form is the point — credentials and MFA stay in the agent's own session, so we never hold or replay them, which is precisely what headless cloud-browser automation cannot say.

Carrier portal terms of use and agency-carrier appointment agreements frequently restrict automated data entry — each carrier target must be cleared individually before shipping, and some will be off-limits, which caps coverage. Also unproven: whether commercial-lines volume at a sub-$500k-revenue agency is high enough to justify $99/user/mo, and whether Relay converts its waitlist into the SMB tier before we ship. If carrier ToS clearance comes back mostly negative, this card dies and PanelFill is the survivor.
